1 Introduction

Many allocation problems in practice are, at their core, instances of dynamic matching with abandonment: participants (or goods) arrive over time and may leave the system before being matched. Consider, for example, kidney exchange programs in which patients with incompatible donors enter a pool over time. Such a program repeatedly searches the pool for pairs that can exchange donors, so that both patients receive compatible kidneys (Roth et al. 2004, Roth et al. 2005, Agarwal et al. 2019, Ashlagi and Roth 2021).11 1 Two-way swaps capture one form of kidney exchange; in practice, programs also arrange longer cycles and chains. A central challenge is to decide which matches to make, as the urgency of each patient’s condition limits how long they can wait in the pool. Timing is even more critical in the allocation of kidneys from deceased donors: a recovered kidney remains viable for at most a day or two and must be discarded if not placed in time (Bertsimas et al. 2013, Agarwal et al. 2021). The same basic problem arises over longer horizons in municipal homeless-response systems. In most major U.S. cities, “Continuum of Care” programs refer people experiencing homelessness to housing opportunities with various providers. These programs must decide which opportunities to offer to which applicants, accounting for compatibility and the possibility that both applicants and housing opportunities might become unavailable over time (Azizi et al. 2018, Arnosti and Simon 2026); similar problems arise in the allocation of public and affordable housing (Arnosti and Shi 2020, Waldinger 2021, Leshno 2022). Beyond these high-stakes settings, online chess and video-game platforms solve a similar problem at a massive scale: within moments, they pair each arriving player, who may log off at any time, with an opponent of comparable strength who is waiting in the lobby (Herbrich et al. 2006, Li et al. 2026). Ride-sharing platforms likewise make real-time matches, pairing riders with nearby drivers before they close the app or choose an alternative platform (Özkan and Ward 2020, Hu and Zhou 2022, Aveklouris et al. 2025).

Despite their differences, all of the above applications share a common structure as centralized matching systems: participants of different types arrive over time, the value of a match depends on the types of both parties and can vary substantially (patients in need of an organ transplant have different expected outcomes from different compatible donors; homeless households might find certain housing opportunities much more attractive than others; and game players generally prefer playing someone of similar skill), and participants may abandon the system if they wait too long (patient health deteriorates, housing applicants disengage, and players log off). Given such a structure, each platform must decide, dynamically and in real time, how to make matching decisions in order to form the best matches before opportunities disappear.

These matching decisions involve two intertwined tradeoffs. The first tradeoff concerns whom to match with whom: the platform must weigh the immediate reward generated from each match against its opportunity cost. Committing an agent to a partner is irreversible and forecloses every other match that either agent might otherwise have formed, potentially with agents that have not yet arrived. Matching well therefore requires correctly valuing scarce agents under uncertainty—that is, balancing the reward collected today against the future value sacrificed (Baccara et al. 2020, Collina et al. 2020). The second tradeoff concerns when to match: delaying available matches allows the market to “thicken” as more agents arrive (Akbarpour et al. 2020, Ashlagi et al. 2023b), but an agent held back for a better match may abandon before such a partner arrives (Kohlenberg 2025).22 2 Deliberate waiting to thicken a market is common in practice, from the periodic match runs of many kidney exchange programs to the batching windows of ride-sharing platforms (Ashlagi et al. 2018, Ashlagi and Roth 2021, Yan et al. 2020, Feng and Niazadeh 2025, Özkan and Ward 2020, Aveklouris et al. 2025). This risk is significant because departure times are typically not known in advance: the platform is uncertain not only about future arrivals but also about how long current participants will remain in the system.

In this paper, we study a fundamental and parsimonious model that captures these tradeoffs: the stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment model, introduced independently by Collina et al. (2020) and Aouad and Sarıtaç (2022), and studied, often in special cases, by many subsequent papers (Kessel et al. 2022, Patel and Wajc 2024, AmaniHamedani et al. 2026, Li et al. 2026). In this model, agents of finitely many types i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T} arrive according to independent Poisson processes—the canonical model for random yet statistically predictable arrivals—with rate λi\lambda_{i} for type ii, and wait in a common pool. Each waiting agent abandons the market after an exponentially distributed sojourn time, at a rate μi\mu_{i} that depends on its type ii. At any moment, the planner may irrevocably match two waiting agents, collecting a reward that depends on their types and on which of the two arrived first: matching an agent of type ii with a later-arriving agent of type jj yields reward ri​jr_{ij}. The planner knows the arrival rates, departure rates, and rewards, and observes arrivals and abandonments as they occur, but does not know the future: an agent’s arrival time is learned when it joins the system, and its departure time is revealed only upon departure, when it is too late to act. The objective is to maximize the long-run average reward.

A key strength of this model is its generality: it captures several important, practically motivated market structures as special cases. In its most general form—in which any two compatible types can match—the model captures kidney exchange and player matchmaking. Splitting the types into two sides, such as supply and demand, and allowing matches only across sides yields two-sided dynamic matching, a market structure studied extensively in operations research (Hu and Zhou 2022, Kohlenberg and Gurvich 2025, Aveklouris et al. 2025). This captures applications such as housing and ride-sharing, where participants on both sides arrive, wait, and may leave unmatched. If, in addition, one side must be matched or discarded immediately upon arrival, this becomes a natural model of organ allocation from deceased donors, as organs must be matched soon after recovery to a waiting patient. This special case, studied by Aouad and Sarıtaç (2022), Patel and Wajc (2024), and AmaniHamedani et al. (2026), among others, is known as stationary bipartite matching. Restricting the waiting side further to a single type—consider, for instance, unit-demand buyers arriving to purchase units of a single good that are replenished and perish over time—yields the (single-good) stationary prophet inequality problem of Kessel et al. (2022), the Markovian continuous-time counterpart of the classical prophet inequality in optimal stopping (Krengel and Sucheston 1978). A guarantee for the general model we study therefore applies to all of these special cases.

1.1 Competitive Analysis and State of the Art

Following the literature on Bayesian online algorithms and stochastic online optimization, we evaluate a matching policy by its competitive ratio against the omniscient benchmark. This benchmark is a “policy” with hindsight information: it knows the times of all arrivals and departures and matches optimally given this information. The competitive ratio of a policy is the worst-case ratio, over all instances (i.e., all possible types, rewards, and arrival and departure rates), between its long-run average reward and that of the omniscient benchmark. It thus measures the fraction of the omniscient benchmark’s reward that can be secured without information about future arrivals and departures.

Prior work shows how demanding this standard is: no online policy can achieve a competitive ratio greater than 12\tfrac{1}{2}, even for the highly restricted single-good stationary prophet inequality problem (Kessel et al. 2022). Whether the ratio of 12\tfrac{1}{2} is achievable has remained open in all but the simplest settings, although a sequence of results has made progressive improvements in various special cases. For the single-good stationary prophet inequality problem, Kessel et al. (2022) designed an optimal 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive policy. For stationary bipartite matching with multiple types on the waiting side, they obtained a ratio of 1556≈0.268\tfrac{15}{56}\approx 0.268; Patel and Wajc (2024) improved this ratio to 1−1e≈0.3931-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{e}}\approx 0.393, and AmaniHamedani et al. (2026) obtained a further small improvement. For the general model, Collina et al. (2020) gave a 18\tfrac{1}{8}-competitive policy, and the best known guarantee is the 0.1920.192-competitive policy of Li et al. (2026).33 3 Li et al. (2026) allow general sojourn-time distributions; with Poisson arrivals, their guarantee of 0.1920.192 requires the variance of each type’s sojourn time to be at most the square of its mean, which holds (with equality) for exponential sojourn times. Their model assumes that the reward of a match does not depend on which agent arrived first. Thus, a substantial gap remains between the best known guarantees and the upper bound of 12\tfrac{1}{2}; Patel and Wajc (2024) posed achieving 12\tfrac{1}{2} as an open question even for the special case of stationary bipartite matching. We should also note that a parallel line of work evaluates policies against the weaker benchmark of the optimal online policy. For the general model, the 0.1920.192 guarantee of Li et al. (2026) against the omniscient benchmark is also the best known guarantee against the optimal online policy, improving the earlier 14​(1−1e)≈0.158\tfrac{1}{4}(1-\tfrac{1}{e})\approx 0.158 guarantee of Aouad and Sarıtaç (2022). Figure 1 summarizes the established guarantees for each setting and benchmark.

Obtaining performance guarantees is challenging, especially without the kind of large-market assumptions used by Özkan and Ward (2020) and Aveklouris et al. (2025). Greedy policies that make every feasible match may match scarce agents with frequent, low-value arrivals. Batching policies, which are common in large-market regimes, may lose impatient agents while the market thickens; in a cost-minimization version of the problem, even optimally tuned batching policies can perform arbitrarily poorly (Aouad and Sarıtaç 2022). Moreover, analyzing the reward obtained by a policy is difficult because the availabilities of different types of agents in the pool are correlated through their shared matching history.

To address these challenges, existing approaches obtain the guarantees above through a common strategy: they first solve a linear programming relaxation (or a variant of it) that prescribes target match rates, and then use these rates to design randomized online policies, such as policies that match with carefully tuned probabilities (Collina et al. 2020, Aouad and Sarıtaç 2022, Kessel et al. 2022, Patel and Wajc 2024, Li et al. 2026). In these papers, randomization plays a key role: it simplifies the analysis and ensures that some matching capacity remains available for favorable future arrivals.

These randomized policies, however, differ sharply from those used in practice, where platforms typically rely on priority rules: coordinated entry systems refer compatible housing applicants in priority order, deceased-donor allocation follows point-based rankings, and matchmaking systems rank feasible opponents (Fajardo 2026, Israni et al. 2014, Graepel and Herbrich 2006). Such rules are deterministic, transparent, and fixed in advance. This gap between theory and practice leads to our central research question: can a simple priority-based policy of the kind practitioners already use attain an optimal performance guarantee? More precisely, we ask the following algorithmic question:

Can a simple priority-based policy, computable in polynomial time, achieve the best possible competitive ratio of 12\tfrac{1}{2} for stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment—in full generality?

1.2 Main Result: Static Priority Policies Offer Optimal Guarantees

We answer this question in the affirmative. We study the simple class of static priority policies.44 4 We borrow this term from the literature on dynamic matching without abandonment, where Kerimov et al. (2025) show that well-designed greedy static priority policies are hindsight optimal in certain matching networks. Such a policy is defined by a ranked list of acceptable partners for each type, and it acts greedily with respect to these lists: an arriving agent is matched to a waiting agent of the highest-ranked acceptable type that is available, and joins the pool if no such agent is available. Here, “static” refers to the fact that priority lists are fixed in advance and do not depend on time, queue lengths, or any other aspect of history; the policy still matches based on which types are available (see Figure 2). Our main result is the following.

Main Result. There is a polynomial-time algorithm that, given any instance of dynamic matching with abandonment, computes a static priority policy whose long-run average reward is at least 12\tfrac{1}{2} of the omniscient benchmark. No online policy can guarantee more.

This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio for general stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment is exactly 12\tfrac{1}{2}, and that a simple deterministic policy attains it. Our result improves the best known guarantee for the general problem from 0.1920.192 to the optimal 12\tfrac{1}{2}, and extends the optimal single-type guarantee of Kessel et al. (2022) to a much larger class of markets—with arbitrarily many types on both sides, non-bipartite compatibility structures, and order-dependent rewards. It achieves the best possible guarantee in every special case considered so far, and closes the central open problem in this line of work, resolving the question of Patel and Wajc (2024) beyond the setting in which it was posed. Since the omniscient benchmark dominates the optimal online policy, our policy also guarantees 12\tfrac{1}{2} of the reward of the optimal online policy, improving upon the best prior guarantees of 0.1920.192 for the general model and about 0.3160.316 for two-sided markets in which both sides may wait.

Managerial insights. Our main result shows that the value of knowing the future in these markets, measured in the worst case over instances, is precisely a factor of two. It is no greater, regardless of the complexity of the instance, and no smaller, regardless of the sophistication of the policy. Furthermore, properly designed priority rules of the kind favored in practice provide optimal worst-case guarantees, which cannot be improved by clever policy design or unbounded computational power. In other words, simplicity entails no loss in worst-case performance.

In fact, we show that the guarantee of 12\tfrac{1}{2} can be achieved by a particularly simple class of static priority policies, which we call value-based policies. Such a policy is described by a single value viv_{i} for each type ii, capturing the opportunity cost of using a waiting agent of that type. (By contrast, a generic static priority policy has a description whose size is quadratic in the number of types.) A match between an agent of type ii and a later-arriving agent of type jj is given the score ri​j−vi−vjr_{ij}-v_{i}-v_{j}. This score is used both to identify acceptable matches (all matches with positive scores, and possibly some with zero score) and to rank them. Our results show that assigning a single number to each type can address the complex tradeoffs identified earlier with no loss to worst-case performance.

1.3 Summary of the Techniques

Given a static priority policy, the numbers of waiting agents of different types evolve as a continuous-time Markov chain. An exact analysis of the policy’s performance would require computing the stationary distribution of this chain. This is difficult because the counts of different types are correlated through their shared history of matches, and their joint distribution depends on the entire collection of priority lists. Our analysis sidesteps this difficulty: it never computes a stationary distribution and instead indirectly certifies the performance of a policy, as discussed below.

An upper bound on the omniscient benchmark. Our starting point is a linear programming relaxation LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} of the omniscient benchmark (Section 2.3), whose variables are the long-run rates of matches between types. Its balance constraints ensure that no type is matched more often than it arrives. Its availability constraints limit how often arrivals of each type can be matched with agents from a given set of types. Such a match requires an agent from the set to be waiting, and since matches only remove agents, an agent from the set is waiting at most as often as in a market where no one is ever matched. In that market, the numbers of waiting agents of different types are independent Poisson random variables, which gives an explicit bound. Similar linear programs appear in prior work. Ours is tighter than those proposed by Collina et al. (2020) and Kessel et al. (2022), which only constrain matches with single types, and it covers a more general setting than the relaxation of AmaniHamedani et al. (2026) for stationary bipartite matching.

Properties of static priority policies and a lower bound on agent availability. These linear programs build on a few observations about static priority policies. Suppose an agent of a given type arrives, and consider a prefix of its ranked list of types. Because these policies match the arriving agent to some type within this prefix whenever at least one type in the prefix is available, the analysis of their reward reduces to a question about agent availability: how often does a given set of types have at least one agent waiting? Calculating this probability exactly is difficult in general, but Section 3 (Lemma 3.3) provides a simple lower bound: the probability that some agent from a set SS is waiting is at least the expected number of waiting agents from SS, times an explicit constant γS\gamma_{S} that depends on the arrival and departure rates but not on the policy. Interestingly, this bound can be viewed as a converse, up to the factor γS\gamma_{S}, to Markov’s inequality.

This is the key stochastic result of the paper. Our proof relies on a property satisfied by static priority policies, which we call independence of irrelevant alternatives: removing a waiting agent from the history does not change what happens to any other agent. Combining this property with the Slivnyak–Mecke formula for Poisson processes, we show that if NSN_{S} is the number of waiting agents with types in SS in steady state, then the conditional distribution of NSN_{S} given NS>0N_{S}>0 is stochastically dominated by the same conditional distribution under the policy that makes no matches, in which NSN_{S} is simply a Poisson random variable; comparing conditional means then yields the bound.

A new family of linear programs to identify a policy and bound its performance. From here, our approach departs from prior work. Rather than using the solution of such a relaxation to define a randomized policy, we use a new family of linear programs, denoted by LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) and indexed by a set ℳ\mathcal{M} of allowed matches, to identify static priority policies. Unlike LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}, these programs are not relaxations. Their values are lower bounds on the rewards of the policies they identify, so each such policy and the omniscient benchmark are squeezed into a “linear programming sandwich,” with LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) below and LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} above. We further show that by properly selecting the set ℳ\mathcal{M} of allowed matches (including the case ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, when all matches are allowed), the optimal objective values of these linear programs never differ by a factor greater than two.

The primal approach: priorities from tight constraints. To design a policy via the above ingredients, our first approach (Section 4) uses the primal LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) directly and reads the priorities from its optimal solution. When the availability constraint of an arriving type and a set of types is tight, the program matches these arrivals with the set as often as the constraint allows, just as a static priority policy does when the set is a prefix of the arriving type’s priority list. This suggests a simple recipe: turn tight sets into prefixes of priority lists. We call a policy consistent with the solution if it follows this recipe and accepts only the matches that the solution uses. We show that every consistent policy earns at least the value of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), even though it may make some matches less often than the program prescribes. Geometrically, the optimal solution lies on a line segment between the policy’s long-run outcome, which need not be feasible, and a feasible solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})—see Figure 5; since the latter earns no more than the optimum, the policy earns no less.

The catch is that a consistent policy may not exist. Using a diminishing-returns (submodularity) property of the availability constraints, we show that the tight sets of each arriving type are nested, so they always fit into a single list. The recipe therefore fails exactly when a tight set contains a type that the solution never matches with the arriving type, since this match would then have to be both accepted and rejected. We call solutions for which the recipe works suitable, and we find one by pruning: starting with all matches allowed, we repeatedly solve LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) and remove the matches that its solution does not use. We show that pruning never lowers the value of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) and ends, after polynomially many rounds, with a suitable optimal solution; the same diminishing-returns property lets us solve each program in polynomial time, despite its exponentially many constraints.

For the set ℳ\mathcal{M} produced by pruning and any policy π\pi that the primal approach constructs from it, our results yield the following chain, where OMN denotes the omniscient benchmark and V⁡(π)V(\pi) the long-run average reward of π\pi:

LPOMN≥OMN≥V⁡(π)≥LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)≥12​LPOMN.\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}\;\geq\;\textup{OMN}\;\geq\;V(\pi)\;\geq\;\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\;\geq\;\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T})\;\geq\;\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}.

The first inequality holds because LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} is a relaxation, and the second because the omniscient benchmark is at least as good as any policy. The last three are the main steps of the primal approach: a consistent policy earns at least the value of its program, pruning never lowers this value, and halving turns any solution of LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} into a solution of LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}). Each inequality may be loose on a given instance; however, their combined loss is at most a factor of two. The primal approach, therefore, yields a 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive policy in polynomial-time.

The dual approach: priorities from values. Our second approach (Section 5) works directly with the value-based policies of Section 1.2, so the question becomes how to set the values. If they are too low, the policy uses up its agents on poor matches; if they are too high, it holds agents back until they abandon. To find the right balance, for every static priority policy π\pi, we introduce a linear program LPLB​(π){\textup{LP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi) that resembles LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) but is tied to π\pi: it is a minimization program, and its availability constraints are flipped and imposed only on the prefixes of the priority lists of π\pi. With these changes, it is easy to see that LPLB​(π){\textup{LP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi) is a lower bound on the long-run average reward V⁡(π)V(\pi) of π\pi. We then use linear programming duality: the dual of LPLB​(π){\textup{LP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi) gives each type a variable that plays the role of its value. Its constraints also identify a set of inequalities that tell us when a vector of values certifies that π\pi earns at least the dual objective ∑iλi​vi\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i} by weak duality. Interestingly, reversing these inequalities—including for the matches that π\pi never makes—gives a certificate in the other direction: we show that values that satisfy the reversed inequalities guarantee that the omniscient benchmark earns at most twice ∑iλi​vi\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}. A tight certificate, which satisfies both sets of inequalities, therefore shows that π\pi earns at least half of the omniscient benchmark.

Which values admit a tight certificate? We show that they are exactly the solutions of a fixed-point equation 𝐯=𝐅⁡(𝐯)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{v}) for a particular piecewise affine map 𝐅\mathbf{F}. In economic terms, the equation balances, for each type, the rate at which a waiting agent loses value to abandonment against a pessimistic estimate of the rate at which its availability creates surplus (positive scores) for later arrivals, in the spirit of the balanced thresholds and prices used for prophet inequalities (Kleinberg and Weinberg 2019, Dütting et al. 2020). The fixed point is also unique and efficiently computable. The map 𝐅\mathbf{F} is not always a contraction, but we show that a damped version of it brings any two vectors of values closer together by a fixed factor under an appropriately weighted norm. Hence, the fixed-point equation has exactly one solution. Moreover, because 𝐅\mathbf{F} is piecewise affine, Ellipsoid-based algorithms for contractions (Sikorski et al. 1993, Daskalakis et al. 2026) find this solution in polynomial time. The dual approach, therefore, yields a 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive value-based policy in polynomial time.

Primal meets dual. One might wonder whether the two approaches above are connected in any way. The primal approach reads priorities from the tight constraints of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), while the dual approach computes them from a fixed point, without solving LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) at all. Despite these differences, it turns out that the two approaches are mathematically linked through the dual of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) (Section 6). This dual assigns a shadow price to each type, and its constraints have the same form as the reversed inequalities of the dual approach, restricted to the matches in ℳ\mathcal{M}. We show that the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}, which solves the fixed-point equation when only the matches in ℳ\mathcal{M} are allowed, is always feasible for this dual. Remarkably, suitability, which the primal approach critically needs to read a policy from an optimal solution, is exactly what turns the shadow prices into fixed-point values: we show that if LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a suitable optimal solution, the optimal shadow prices are unique and equal 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}, so solving the dual recovers the restricted fixed point. We also show by an example that, without suitability, they need not solve this equation.

For the set ℳ\mathcal{M} produced by pruning, the connection extends to policies. Through complementary slackness, we show that every policy that the primal approach constructs is indeed a value-based policy restricted to ℳ\mathcal{M}: it ranks the matches in ℳ\mathcal{M} by their scores under 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}. The primal approach is thus a value-based approach in disguise, even though it never computes a value. Notably, this restricted value-based policy may differ from the unrestricted value-based policy of the dual approach, but it is still a 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive policy, as explained earlier.

As a byproduct of the above investigation, we identify a broader class of (restricted) value-based policies that includes the policies of both approaches as special cases. Specifically, for every set of allowed matches ℳ\mathcal{M} with LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}), we show that every value-based policy restricted to ℳ\mathcal{M} whose values are the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} earns at least half of the omniscient benchmark. The policies of the dual approach are exactly the members of this class with ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}. The set produced by pruning also satisfies LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}), so, by the value-based interpretation above, every policy of the primal approach is also a member of this class. We view this class as a unifying lens on our two approaches and believe that it may be of independent interest.

1.4 Organization

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 includes the model, preliminaries, and backgrounds. Section 3 defines static priority policies and establishes their key properties, including our lower bound on agent availability (Lemma 3.3). Section 4 presents the primal approach, Section 5 presents the dual approach, and Section 6 connects the two approaches through the primal-dual lens. Section 7 concludes. The appendices contain a discussion of further related work in operations research, economics, and computer science (Appendix A), the definitions and proofs for Poisson processes (Appendix B), the omitted proofs (Appendix C), and additional examples (Appendix D).

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we define our model (Section 2.1), state some key facts about Poisson processes that our analysis uses (Section 2.2), and introduce the omniscient benchmark and a linear programming relaxation that upper-bounds it (Section 2.3).

2.1 Model and Notation

We study the continuous-time model of stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment introduced by Collina et al. (2020) and Aouad and Sarıtaç (2022). This model has Poisson arrivals, exponential departures, and pairwise matching. Formally, an instance is a tuple ℐ=(𝒯,𝝀,𝝁,𝐫)\mathcal{I}=(\mathcal{T},\bm{\lambda},\bm{\mu},\mathbf{r}), where

  • •

    𝒯\mathcal{T} is a finite set of agent types.

  • •

    𝝀∈ℝ>0𝒯\bm{\lambda}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{T}} specifies agent arrival rates. Agents of each type arrive according to Poisson processes that are independent across types, with λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 denoting the arrival rate of type i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T}.

  • •

    𝝁∈ℝ>0𝒯\bm{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\mathcal{T}} specifies departure rates. Each agent has a maximum sojourn time (or simply sojourn time), after which the agent will abandon the system if not matched. These times are independent of each other and of the arrival processes, and exponentially distributed. The expected maximum sojourn time for an agent of type i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T} is 1/μi1/\mu_{i}.

  • •

    𝐫∈ℝ≥0𝒯×𝒯\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}} specifies matching rewards. Each match involves a pair of agents. For any i,j∈𝒯i,j\in\mathcal{T}, ri​j≥0r_{ij}\geq 0 specifies the planner’s reward for the match (i,j)(i,j), that is, from matching an agent of type ii to an agent of type jj who arrived later. We allow ri​j≠rj​ir_{ij}\neq r_{ji}, so the reward may depend on which agent has waited longer. (Since arrivals follow independent Poisson processes, almost surely no two agents arrive at the same time.)

For t≥0t\geq 0 and i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T}, let 𝒜i​(t)\mathcal{A}_{i}(t) be the set of type-ii agents that have arrived before time tt, and 𝒜⁡(t)=⋃i∈𝒯𝒜i​(t)\mathcal{A}(t)=\bigcup_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{A}_{i}(t) the set of all arrivals. For an agent aa, let iai_{a} denote its type, tat_{a} denote its arrival time, sas_{a} denote its maximum sojourn time, and da=ta+sad_{a}=t_{a}+s_{a} denote the time at which aa will depart if not matched. We next define the notions of present and available agents.

Definition 2.1 (Present/available agents).

An agent aa is present at time tt if ta≤t<dat_{a}\leq t<d_{a}, that is, if it has arrived and has not reached its departure time. Under an online policy, which is a policy that makes irrevocable matches over time (see below), an agent is available at time tt if it is present and has not yet been matched.

These definitions of present and available are consistent with the use of these terms in past work—see, for example Kessel et al. (2022), Patel and Wajc (2024). Presence depends only on the arrival and departure times, and not on the matching policy. Availability, in contrast, depends on the policy: a present agent stops being available as soon as the policy matches it.

We now define matching policies formally. The history up to time tt,

ℋ⁡(t)={(ia,ta,da)}a∈𝒜⁡(t),\mathcal{H}(t)=\{(i_{a},t_{a},d_{a})\}_{a\in\mathcal{A}(t)},

records the type, arrival time, and departure time of every agent that has arrived before time tt; for notational simplicity, it includes departure times that occur after tt. From the history ℋ⁡(t)\mathcal{H}(t), we define the compatibility graph G⁡(t)G(t) with vertices 𝒜⁡(t)\mathcal{A}(t), and an edge between agents aa and bb if there is a time at which they are both present. Each edge has a weight, which is simply the reward earned from matching the two agents involved. A matching of G⁡(t)G(t) is a subset of edges with no two edges sharing a vertex, and its weight is the sum of the rewards on those edges.

Given the above primitives, a policy with hindsight information is a function π\pi that maps each history ℋ⁡(t)\mathcal{H}(t) to a matching of G⁡(t)G(t). This definition allows the policy to make decisions for early arrivals based on future arrival and departure information, and does not require the policy to be consistent across horizons.55 5 For instance, if only two agents have arrived by time tt, a policy may match them to each other when optimizing for horizon tt, yet leave them for other partners when optimizing for a later horizon. This gives great power to our omniscient benchmark, while static priority policies do not use this power. An online policy, in contrast, makes irrevocable matches between available agents (Definition 2.1) using only the information revealed so far: the types and arrival times of the agents that have arrived, and the departures that have already occurred. In particular, it learns the departure time of an agent only when the agent abandons. The matches that an online policy—possibly randomized—makes during [0,t][0,t] form a matching of G⁡(t)G(t) in each realization.66 6 Models that instead reveal when an agent is about to abandon (Akbarpour et al. 2020, Huang et al. 2020a), or that disallow abandonment altogether (Kerimov et al. 2025), differ substantially from ours; see Appendix A.

Fix a policy π\pi, types i,j∈𝒯i,j\in\mathcal{T} and a horizon t>0t>0. Let Xi​jπ​(t)X_{ij}^{\pi}(t) denote the number of (i,j)(i,j) matches that π\pi makes during [0,t][0,t] (which is a random variable). Let xi​jπ​(t)x_{ij}^{\pi}(t) be the corresponding expected match rate over the period [0,t][0,t], where the expectation is over the arrival and abandonment processes:

Xi​jπ​(t)\displaystyle X_{ij}^{\pi}(t) =|{(a,b)∈π(ℋ(t)):ia=i,ib=j,ta<tb}|,\displaystyle=\big|\{(a,b)\in\pi(\mathcal{H}(t)):i_{a}=i,\ i_{b}=j,\ t_{a}<t_{b}\}\big|,
xi​jπ​(t)\displaystyle x_{ij}^{\pi}(t) =1t​𝔼​[Xi​jπ​(t)].\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{t}\mathbb{E}\left[X_{ij}^{\pi}(t)\right]. (1)

From this, we can compute the expected reward rate of π\pi on [0,t][0,t],

V⁡(π,t)=∑i,j∈𝒯ri​j​xi​jπ​(t).V(\pi,t)=\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{T}}r_{ij}x_{ij}^{\pi}(t). (2)

We evaluate a policy by its long-run average reward V⁡(π)=lim inft→∞V⁡(π,t)V(\pi)=\liminf_{t\to\infty}V(\pi,t); for the static priority policies of Section 3, this limit exists (Lemma 3.1).

2.2 Background on Poisson Processes

Our analysis relies on three results about Poisson processes, which we collect here. Appendix B contains the formal definition of a Poisson process and some associated proofs. Informally, a Poisson process on a set 𝒳⊆ℝn\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} with rate function λ⁡(⋅)\lambda(\cdot) is a random collection of points in 𝒳\mathcal{X} such that the numbers of points in disjoint regions are independent Poisson random variables, and the expected number of points in a region is the integral of λ⁡(⋅)\lambda(\cdot) over that region (Definition B.1). In our model, the arrival times of type-ii agents form a Poisson process on [0,∞)[0,\infty) with constant rate λi\lambda_{i}.

The first result concerns the agents that are present at a given time. It follows from the marking property of Poisson processes (Fact B.1 in Appendix B), which, applied to the arrivals of type ii with their sojourn times as marks, shows that the pairs of arrival times and sojourn times of type-ii agents form a Poisson process on [0,∞)2[0,\infty)^{2} with rate function (s,ℓ)↦λi​μi​e−μi​ℓ(s,\ell)\mapsto\lambda_{i}\mu_{i}e^{-\mu_{i}\ell}.

Lemma 2.1.

The number of type-ii agents present at time tt is Poisson with mean

λiμi​(1−e−μi​t).\tfrac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}\big(1-e^{-\mu_{i}t}\big).

These counts are independent across types.

Since presence does not depend on the policy, and an agent can be available only if it is present, this lemma limits the availability of agents under every policy. We prove it in Appendix B.

The second result is a formula for the expected value of a sum over the points of a Poisson process (Slivnyak 1962, Mecke 1967); see also Last and Penrose (2017, Theorem 4.1). Intuitively, it says that, conditional on a Poisson process having a point at a given location, the other points still form a Poisson process with the same rate function. Below, 𝒩⁡(𝒳)\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X}) denotes the collection of locally finite subsets of 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

Fact 2.1 (Campbell–Mecke formula, Mecke equation, or Slivnyak–Mecke formula).

Let Φ\Phi be a Poisson process on a Borel set 𝒳⊆ℝn\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} with rate function λ⁡(x)\lambda(x), and let g:𝒳×𝒩⁡(𝒳)→ℝ≥0g:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X})\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be a measurable function of a distinguished point and a point set. Then

𝔼⁡[∑x∈Φg⁡(x,Φ∖{x})]=∫𝒳𝔼⁡[g⁡(x,Φ)]​λ​(x)​𝑑x.\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{x\in\Phi}g(x,\Phi\setminus\{x\})\right]=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[g(x,\Phi)\right]\lambda(x)dx.

Fact 2.1 is the main tool in the proof of our key stochastic result, Lemma 3.3 in Section 3. Together with the marking property (Fact B.1), it also implies the third result, which is known as PASTA, for “Poisson arrivals see time averages” (Wolff 1982): in the long run, the fraction of arrivals of a given type that find the system in a given set of states equals the fraction of time that the system spends in these states. To state it, for an online policy π\pi, let Niπ​(t)N^{\pi}_{i}(t) be the number of type-ii agents available just before time tt, and let 𝐍π​(t)=(Niπ​(t))i∈𝒯\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t)=(N^{\pi}_{i}(t))_{i\in\mathcal{T}} be the state of the system.

Corollary 2.2 (PASTA).

Let π\pi be an online policy, and fix a type jj and a set of states CC. Then for every t≥0t\geq 0,

𝔼⁡[∑a∈𝒜j​(t)(𝐍π​(ta)∈C)]=λj​∫0tℙ⁡(𝐍π​(s)∈C)​𝑑s.\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{j}(t)}\mathbf{1}\!\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t_{a})\in C\right)\right]=\lambda_{j}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(s)\in C\right)ds.

In particular, if ℙ⁡(𝐍π​(s)∈C)→p\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(s)\in C\right)\to p as s→∞s\to\infty, then

limt→∞𝔼⁡[∑a∈𝒜j​(t)(𝐍π​(ta)∈C)]t=λj​p.\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{j}(t)}\mathbf{1}\!\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t_{a})\in C\right)\right]}{t}=\lambda_{j}p.

2.3 Benchmark and Guarantee

The omniscient benchmark.

We evaluate policies by comparing their long-run average reward against an omniscient benchmark: the offline optimum that observes the entire realized sequence of arrivals and abandonments and matches optimally in hindsight. For each horizon tt, the largest reward attainable by time tt is the weight of a maximum-weight matching of the compatibility graph G⁡(t)G(t); see Figure 3 for an illustration.

Definition 2.2 (Omniscient benchmark).

For an instance ℐ\mathcal{I} and time t>0t>0, let OMN​(t)\textup{OMN}(t) be the expected weight of a maximum-weight matching of G⁡(t)G(t), divided by tt. The omniscient benchmark is OMN=lim supt→∞OMN​(t)\textup{OMN}=\limsup_{t\to\infty}\textup{OMN}(t).

Because any matching policy must choose a matching of G⁡(t)G(t), the omniscient benchmark bounds the performance of any policy, including the optimal online policy.

Definition 2.3 (Competitive ratio).

A policy π\pi is cc-competitive, for c∈[0,1]c\in[0,1], if for every instance ℐ\mathcal{I}, V⁡(π)≥c⋅OMNV(\pi)\geq c\cdot\textup{OMN}. Its competitive ratio is the largest cc for which this guarantee holds, infℐV⁡(π)/OMN\inf_{\mathcal{I}}V(\pi)/\textup{OMN}.

Our goal is to find an online policy whose competitive ratio is as large as possible.

A linear programming relaxation of the benchmark.

The benchmark OMN is itself difficult to analyze—it is the expected weight of a maximum-weight matching of a random graph—so we work instead with the linear program below, which upper-bounds it. The program has one variable xi​j≥0x_{ij}\geq 0 per ordered pair of types, interpreted as the long-run rate of (i,j)(i,j) matches.

With these variables, Constraint (OMN-Supply) is a flow-balance constraint; in particular, the total rate of matches involving type-jj agents is no more than the rate λj\lambda_{j} for arrivals of type-jj agents.77 7 As we will see in Section 3, this constraint in the equality from—which can be equivalently derived by introducing new variables 𝜶\bm{\alpha} for its non-negative slack, where αj\alpha_{j} is interpreted as the total rate at which type-jj agents leave unmatched—parallels the balance equation of static priority policies. Constraint (OMN-Presence) bounds the rate at which arriving type-jj agents are matched with earlier arrivals whose types are in SS. The following proposition shows that LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} upper-bounds the omniscient benchmark. We sketch its proof below and postpone the full proof to Section C.1.

Proposition 2.3.

For every instance ℐ\mathcal{I}, OMN≤LPOMN\textup{OMN}\leq\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}.

Proof sketch.

It suffices to show that for every policy π\pi (even with hindsight information) and every horizon tt, the match rates xi​jπ​(t)x_{ij}^{\pi}(t) satisfy (OMN-Supply) and (OMN-Presence). Constraint (OMN-Supply) holds because each agent is matched at most once, so the rate of matches involving type-jj agents is at most λj\lambda_{j}; the variable αj\alpha_{j} fills the slack. Turning to (OMN-Presence), an arriving type-jj agent can contribute to the left side of (OMN-Presence) only if some earlier arrival with a type in SS is still present upon its arrival. By Lemma 2.1 (see Section 2.2), the number of type-ii agents present at time ss is Poisson with mean λiμi​(1−e−μi​s)≤λi/μi\tfrac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}(1-e^{-\mu_{i}s})\leq\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i}, independently across types. Since a sum of independent Poisson random variables is Poisson, the probability that no earlier arrival with a type in SS is present at time ss is at least e−∑i∈Sλi/μie^{-\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i}}. By Corollary B.1, a version of PASTA property (Corollary 2.2) for events that depend on the history up to any arbitrary time tt, the expected number of type-jj agents that arrive during [0,t][0,t] and find some earlier arrival with a type in SS still available (and hence present) is therefore at most λjt(1−e−∑i∈Sλi/μi)\lambda_{j}t\big(1-e^{-\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i}}\big). Dividing by tt gives (OMN-Presence). ∎

The relaxation LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} is tighter than those used in prior work, which bound matches with only one type at a time: Kessel et al. (2022) use the singleton cases |S|=1|S|=1 of (OMN-Presence), and Collina et al. (2020) use a weaker form of these singleton constraints. Constraints for larger sets matter: an arriving agent can be matched with at most one partner, and the probability that some type in SS is present can be much smaller than the sum of the probabilities that each type in SS is present. The work of AmaniHamedani et al. (2026) allows for all subsets SS, but assumes a restricted setting where types are partitioned into two sides, all valid matches involve one type from each side, and one side must be matched immediately upon arrival.

3 Static Priority Policies

We now introduce the class of simple deterministic policies that are the focus of this paper. Formally, a static priority policy π\pi specifies, for each type j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T}, a strict order ≻j\succ_{j} over 𝒯∪{∅}\mathcal{T}\cup\{\emptyset\}, called the priority list of type jj. We say that type ii is acceptable to type jj if i≻j∅i\succ_{j}\emptyset, and let

ℳ(π)={(i,j):i≻j∅}\mathcal{M}(\pi)=\{(i,j):i\succ_{j}\emptyset\}

be the set of acceptable matches. The policy will never make an unacceptable match.

Recall from Definition 2.1 that an agent is available at time tt if it is present and has not yet been matched. We say that a type is available if there is an available agent of that type. When an agent of type jj arrives, the policy matches this agent to the acceptable and available type with the highest priority (according to ≻j\succ_{j}). If no acceptable type is available, the arriving agent joins the pool and waits. Therefore, every match made by a static priority policy pairs a newly arrived agent with a waiting agent (two waiting agents are never matched to each other). Ties among available agents of the same type are broken by an arbitrary but fixed rule.88 8 For example, among agents of a given type, we might match the earliest arrival. The choice of tie-breaking rule does not affect any of our analysis or results, which depend only on the number of available agents of each type 𝐍π\mathbf{N}^{\pi}. Figure 4 illustrates how a static priority policy operates on a simple example.

Steady state.

Under a static priority policy, whether a match occurs depends only on which types are currently available, so the count of available agents of each type evolves as a Markov process. Let Niπ​(t)N_{i}^{\pi}(t) be the number of type-ii agents available just before time tt, as in Section 2.2. We refer to 𝐍π​(t)=(Niπ​(t))i∈𝒯\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t)=(N_{i}^{\pi}(t))_{i\in\mathcal{T}} as the state. We show that this state converges to a stationary distribution.

Lemma 3.1.

For any static priority policy π\pi, the state 𝐍π​(t)\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t) is a continuous-time Markov chain. This chain is ergodic, and has a unique stationary distribution. Therefore, the following limits exist:

niπ≜limt→∞𝔼⁡[Niπ​(t)],xi​jπ≜limt→∞1t​𝔼​[Xi​jπ​(t)],V⁡(π)≜limt→∞V⁡(π,t)n_{i}^{\pi}\triangleq\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}^{\pi}(t)\right],\quad x_{ij}^{\pi}\mathrel{\triangleq}\lim_{t\to\infty}\tfrac{1}{t}\mathbb{E}\left[X_{ij}^{\pi}(t)\right],\quad V(\pi)\triangleq\lim_{t\to\infty}V(\pi,t) (3)

These quantities will be our key summary statistics of interest. The quantity niπn_{i}^{\pi} is the expected (or average) number of available agents of type ii. Meanwhile, the quantity xi​jπx_{ij}^{\pi} is the long-run rate at which the policy makes (i,j)(i,j) matches. The full proofs of the results of this section are in Section C.2.

We now identify some key properties of static priority policies. These will be used to motivate two novel families of linear programs: LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) (in Section 4) and LPLB​(π){\textup{LP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi) (in Section 5). We then use these linear programs to identify a good policy and bound its performance.

Definition 3.1 (Prefix).

A set S⊆𝒯S\subseteq\mathcal{T} is a prefix of an order ≻\succ over 𝒯∪{∅}\mathcal{T}\cup\{\emptyset\} if there is an acceptable type i≻∅i\succ\emptyset with S={i′∈𝒯:i′⪰i}S=\{i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}:i^{\prime}\succeq i\}. We write Prefixes​(≻)\text{Prefixes}(\succ) for the collection of all prefixes of ≻\succ, and for a static priority policy π={≻j}j∈𝒯\pi=\{\succ_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}} we write 𝒫j(π)=Prefixes(≻j)\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi)=\text{Prefixes}(\succ_{j}).

Lemma 3.2.

Let π={≻j}j∈𝒯\pi=\{\succ_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}} be a static priority policy and let 𝐍π\mathbf{N}^{\pi} be drawn from its stationary distribution. Then the following hold:

V⁡(π)=∑i,j∈𝒯ri​j​xi​jπ\displaystyle V(\pi)=\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{T}}r_{ij}x_{ij}^{\pi} (4)
njπ​μj+∑i∈𝒯xi​jπ+∑i∈𝒯xj​iπ=λj\displaystyle n_{j}^{\pi}\mu_{j}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}x_{ij}^{\pi}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}x_{ji}^{\pi}=\lambda_{j} ∀j∈𝒯,\displaystyle\forall j\in\mathcal{T}, (SP-Balance)
∑i∈Sxi​jπ≤λj​ℙ​(∑i∈SNiπ>0)\displaystyle\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij}^{\pi}\leq\lambda_{j}\mathbb{P}\left(\textstyle\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi}>0\right) ∀j∈𝒯,S⊆𝒯.\displaystyle\forall j\in\mathcal{T},\ S\subseteq\mathcal{T}. (SP-Availability)

Moreover, (SP-Availability) holds with equality whenever S∈Prefixes(≻j)S\in\text{Prefixes}(\succ_{j}).

Proof sketch.

Most of the proof follows the same lines as in the proof of Proposition 2.3. For constraint (SP-Balance), note that every arriving agent of type ii eventually matches or abandons the system. Because departures follow an exponential distribution and are not known in advance, the long-run rate of total departure from the system is the average number of available agents niπn_{i}^{\pi}, multiplied by the departure rate μi\mu_{i}. The rate of matches is ∑j∈𝒯(xi​jπ+xj​iπ)\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\big(x_{ij}^{\pi}+x_{ji}^{\pi}\big). Adding these together, therefore, gives the arrival rate of type-ii agents. For (SP-Availability), an arriving type-jj agent can match into SS and contribute to the left side of the constraint only if some agent of a type in SS is available upon its arrival. This happens with probability ℙ⁡(∑i∈SNiπ>0)\mathbb{P}\left(\textstyle\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi}>0\right), by PASTA (Corollary 2.2). Multiplying by the arrival rate of type-jj agents gives (SP-Availability). If SS is a prefix, then if some agent of a type in SS is available, jj must match with such an agent. This gives the equality. ∎

Lemma 3.2—and (SP-Availability) in particular—says that a key to analyzing the performance of a static priority policy is understanding the probability with which various sets of types are available. This can be quite challenging, as availability is correlated across types. However, our next result establishes a lower bound on the probability that a type from SS is available, expressed in terms of the expected number of available agents from this set; notably, the expected number of available type-jj agents is connected to the total departure rate of type jj (through a linear function in the case of exponential departures), which itself is connected to matching rates 𝐱π\mathbf{x}^{\pi} via (SP-Balance).

To state this lower bound, for S⊆𝒯S\subseteq\mathcal{T} write ρ⁡(S)=∑i∈Sλi/μi\rho(S)=\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i} and define

γS≜1−e−ρ⁡(S)ρ⁡(S)=1−e−∑i∈Sλi/μi∑i∈Sλi/μi.\gamma_{S}\triangleq\frac{1-e^{-\rho(S)}}{\rho(S)}=\frac{1-e^{-\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i}}}{\sum_{i\in S}\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i}}. (5)

For S=∅S=\emptyset, we set γ∅=1\gamma_{\emptyset}=1, the limit of this expression as ρ⁡(S)→0\rho(S)\to 0.

Lemma 3.3.

Let π={≻j}j∈𝒯\pi=\{\succ_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}} be any static priority policy and let 𝐍π\mathbf{N}^{\pi} be drawn from its stationary distribution. Then for every S⊆𝒯S\subseteq\mathcal{T},

ℙ⁡(∑i∈SNiπ>0)≥γS​∑i∈Sniπ.\mathbb{P}\left(\textstyle\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi}>0\right)\geq\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}^{\pi}. (6)

This is the key stochastic result of our work. There are several ways to interpret it. One interpretation is as a sort of converse to Markov’s inequality, which states that the probability that a random variable on ℕ\mathbb{N} is positive is at most its expectation. Inequality (6) shows that this expectation also serves as a lower bound after multiplying by the constant γS\gamma_{S}. Another observation is that if the policy chooses never to match types in SS, then (6) holds with equality. Thus, the conditional expectation of the number of available agents from SS, given that this number is at least one, is maximized by the policy that makes no matches. There is also a conceptual connection to the literature on prophet inequalities, which often uses arguments of the flavor “either item ii matches with high probability, or it is likely to be available to match with other items” (see, for example, Lucier 2017). Lemma 3.3 gives an analogous conclusion for the stationary setting that we consider: if agents from SS are unlikely to be available (the left side of (6) is small), then it must be that they are matching at high rates (each niπn_{i}^{\pi} is small).

We defer the full proof of Lemma 3.3 to Section C.2, and sketch main ideas next.

Proof sketch of Lemma 3.3.

The proof relies solely on a property of static priority policies that we call independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) (formally in Definition C.1): if an agent aa is available at time tt, then removing aa from the history does not change what happens to any other agent, so the only effect on the state at time tt is that the number of available agents of aa’s type decreases by one. Let 𝐍π\mathbf{N}^{\pi} be the “stationary state” of the policy π\pi satisfying IIA. The main step is showing the following inequality, which holds for every type ii and every set CC of states:

𝔼⁡[Niπ​(𝐍π−𝐞i∈C)]≤λiμi​ℙ​(𝐍π∈C),\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}^{\pi}\,\mathbf{1}\!\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}-\mathbf{e}_{i}\in C\right)\right]\;\leq\;\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}\,\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}\in C\right),

where 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} is the ii-th unit vector. We first prove this inequality at a fixed time tt, with 𝐍π​(t)\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t) in place of 𝐍π\mathbf{N}^{\pi}, and then let t→∞t\to\infty. Intuitively, the left side is the steady-state (or limit) value of the expected number of available type-ii agents whose removal from the history ℋ⁡(t)\mathcal{H}(t) would leave the system in a state in CC. By IIA, removing one agent does not change other agents in distribution. Then, the Slivnyak–Mecke formula (Fact 2.1) finds another way of counting this expected number by turning the expectation into an integral over the arrival and sojourn times (s,ℓ)(s,\ell) of an extra type-ii agent added to the system, with respect to the rate function λi​μi​e−μi​ℓ\lambda_{i}\mu_{i}e^{-\mu_{i}\ell} of these times (Section 2.2). The integrand is the probability that this agent is available at time tt while the system without it is in a state in CC. Since the extra agent can be available only if it is present, this integral is at most ℙ​(𝐍π​(t)∈C)\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t)\in C\right) times the expected number of type-ii agents present at time tt, which is at most λi/μi\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i} by Lemma 2.1.

Now fix a nonempty set S⊆𝒯S\subseteq\mathcal{T}, let NS=∑i∈SNiπN_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi} and pm=ℙ⁡(NS=m)p_{m}=\mathbb{P}\left(N_{S}=m\right), and apply the inequality with CC the set of states in which exactly mm available agents have types in SS. By summing over i∈Si\in S,

(m+1)​pm+1≤ρ⁡(S)​pmfor all ​m≥0,(m+1)\,p_{m+1}\;\leq\;\rho(S)\,p_{m}\qquad\text{for all }m\geq 0,

simply because removing a type-ii agent leaves the system in a state in CC if and only if NS=m+1N_{S}=m+1. A Poisson random variable LSL_{S} with mean ρ⁡(S)\rho(S) satisfies this recurrence with equality; NSN_{S} has this distribution in steady state when agents with types in SS are never matched, because such agents are then available whenever they are present (Lemma 2.1). Comparing the two recurrences shows that the ratio pm/ℙ⁡(LS=m)p_{m}/\mathbb{P}\left(L_{S}=m\right) is nonincreasing in mm, so that the conditional distribution of NSN_{S} given NS>0N_{S}>0 is stochastically dominated by that of LSL_{S} given LS>0L_{S}>0. In particular,

𝔼⁡[NS]ℙ⁡(NS>0)=𝔼⁡[NS∣NS>0]≤𝔼⁡[LS∣LS>0]=ρ⁡(S)1−e−ρ⁡(S)=1γS.\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[N_{S}\right]}{\mathbb{P}\left(N_{S}>0\right)}=\mathbb{E}\left[N_{S}\mid N_{S}>0\right]\;\leq\;\mathbb{E}\left[L_{S}\mid L_{S}>0\right]=\frac{\rho(S)}{1-e^{-\rho(S)}}=\frac{1}{\gamma_{S}}.

Since 𝔼⁡[NS]=∑i∈Sniπ\mathbb{E}\left[N_{S}\right]=\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}^{\pi}, rearranging gives (6). ∎

Together, (SP-Balance), (SP-Availability), and Lemma 3.3 are the only properties of static priority policies that we use. In the next sections, they let us construct families of linear programs whose solutions both identify a static priority policy and lower-bound its reward. In fact, from here we give two approaches for identifying a static priority policy that earns at least 12​OMN\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{OMN}:

  1. (i)

    In Section 4, we introduce a new family of linear programs indexed by a set ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T} of allowed matches. Their constraints mirror (SP-Balance) and (SP-Availability) (restricted to ℳ\mathcal{M}), with the probability in (SP-Availability) replaced by its lower bound from Lemma 3.3. Given a solution to an LP in this family, we draw inspiration from Lemma 3.2, designing a static priority policy such that tight constraints all correspond to prefixes of the priority list ≻j\succ_{j}. (Intuitively, if the constraint corresponding to SS and jj is tight, then the linear program is trying to make as many matches as possible between arriving type jj agents and waiting agents from the set SS, so types in SS should appear at the “top” of ≻j\succ_{j}.)

    We show that any policy consistent with an optimal solution of an LP in this family earns a long-run average reward of at least the LP value. We then provide a polynomial-time algorithm to find a set ℳ\mathcal{M} such that a consistent policy with respect to an optimal solution of the LP corresponding to ℳ\mathcal{M} exists, and this LP value is at least 12​OMN\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{OMN}.

  2. (ii)

    In Section 5, we explore an especially simple class of static priority policies, called value-based policies, which assign a value viv_{i} to each type ii, interpreted as the “opportunity cost” of matching that type. These policies prioritize matches based on their “score” ri​j−vi−vjr_{ij}-v_{i}-v_{j}. Matches with negative scores are unacceptable, and matches with positive scores are acceptable.

    To find an appropriate choice of 𝐯\mathbf{v}, we introduce a linear program that lower-bounds the reward of a given static priority policy π\pi. Taking the dual of this program establishes conditions on 𝐯\mathbf{v} that ensure that the long-run average reward of π\pi is at least ∑i∈𝒯λi​vi\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v_{i}. Meanwhile, taking the dual of LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} establishes complementary conditions on 𝐯\mathbf{v} that ensure that ∑i∈𝒯λi​vi\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v_{i} is at least 12​OMN\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{OMN}. Finding a 𝐯\mathbf{v} that satisfies both sets of conditions simultaneously comes down to solving a particular fixed-point equation, which we show has a unique solution that is computable in polynomial time.

Although the two approaches above seem quite different, as we show later in Section 6, there are deep connections between the two, and they are mathematically linked via linear programming duality.

4 Primal Approach

In this section, we introduce a family of linear programs LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), indexed by a set ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T} of allowed matches. We use these linear programs both to identify a static priority policy and to lower-bound its performance.

This is how this section is organized: Section 4.1 introduces LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) and shows that the value of LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) is at least half of LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}, and hence of the omniscient benchmark (Proposition 4.1). Section 4.2 describes how to identify a static priority policy from an optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}): Proposition 4.2 establishes that any static priority policy that is consistent with such a solution earns a long-run average reward of at least LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Unfortunately, an optimal solution of LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) might not be suitable, meaning that no static priority policy is consistent with it. Section 4.3 addresses this concern with a pruning algorithm that finds a set ℳ\mathcal{M} such that LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a suitable optimal solution and LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}). It also shows that LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) can be solved in polynomial time, despite its exponentially many constraints.

4.1 A Novel Family of Linear Programs

Our linear program is inspired by the objective (4) and by the constraints (SP-Balance) and (SP-Availability) of static priority policies (Lemma 3.2). The decision variables are 𝐧=(ni)i∈𝒯{\bf n}=(n_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{T}} (with nin_{i} interpreted as the expected number of available type-ii agents) and 𝐱=(xi​j)(i,j)∈ℳ{\bf x}=(x_{ij})_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}} (with xi​jx_{ij} interpreted as the rate of (i,j)(i,j) matches). Given any set ℳ\mathcal{M} of allowed matches, define ℳj={i:(i,j)∈ℳ}\mathcal{M}_{j}=\{i:(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}\} to be the set of types that an arriving type-jj agent may be matched with, and define LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})—referred to as the policy LP—as follows.

We now give some intuition for LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), comparing it first to the constraints (SP-Balance) and (SP-Availability) satisfied by static priority policies, and then to the constraints (OMN-Supply) and (OMN-Presence) that define our upper bound LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}.

Comparing (P-Balance) and (P-Availability) with their counterparts (SP-Balance) and (SP-Availability), the only difference is that the probability ℙ⁡(∑i∈SNiπ>0)\mathbb{P}(\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi}>0)—that some type in SS is available—which appears in (SP-Availability), has been replaced by the linear term γS​∑i∈Sni\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}n_{i} in (P-Availability). This replacement is motivated by Lemma 3.3, which says that, for static priority policies, ℙ⁡(∑i∈SNiπ>0)\mathbb{P}(\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi}>0) is always at least γS​∑i∈Sniπ\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}^{\pi}. Thus, (P-Availability) is a tightening of the corresponding constraint satisfied by static priority policies. In Section 4.2, this will be the key fact used to show that the value of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) is a lower bound on the reward of any static priority policy consistent with an optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}).

For now, we turn to a different goal: relating the value of LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) to LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}. There is a clear correspondence between (OMN-Supply) and (P-Balance): given any 𝐱{\bf x} that satisfies (OMN-Supply), simply define 𝐧{\bf n} so that (P-Balance) holds, that is, nj​μj=αjn_{j}\mu_{j}=\alpha_{j}. Thus, nj​μjn_{j}\mu_{j} is the difference between the arrival rate and the match rate of type jj, that is, the rate at which type-jj agents abandon the system. The meaningful difference between LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} and LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) is the replacement of (OMN-Presence) with (P-Availability). Applying the definition of γS\gamma_{S} in (5), the right side of (P-Availability) can be written as

λj​(1−e−ρ⁡(S))​∑i∈Sniρ⁡(S).\lambda_{j}(1-e^{-\rho(S)})\frac{\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}}{\rho(S)}.

This is simply the right side of (OMN-Presence), times a fraction that is at most one. (To see that the fraction is at most one, note that (P-Balance) ensures that each ni≤λi/μin_{i}\leq\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i}; conceptually this makes sense, as nin_{i} represents the expected number of available agents, while λi/μi\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i} is the expected number of present agents.) As a result, for any feasible 𝐧{\bf n}, (P-Availability) is a tighter constraint than (OMN-Presence), and thus LPPOL​(ℳ)≤LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\leq\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}.

The constraint (P-Availability) also captures the following intuition. Matched agents are no longer available, so the more often a policy matches type-ii agents, the fewer type-ii agents are available, on average, when other agents arrive. The right side of (OMN-Presence) ignores this effect, since it does not depend on how often agents are matched. In (P-Availability) with S={i}S=\{i\}, by contrast, the fraction that multiplies the right side of (OMN-Presence) is ni​μi/λin_{i}\mu_{i}/\lambda_{i}, which by (P-Balance) is the fraction of type-ii agents that abandon rather than match. Thus, the higher the match rate of type-ii agents, the smaller nin_{i} becomes, resulting in a tighter availability constraint (P-Availability).

Although LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)≤LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T})\leq\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}, it cannot be too much smaller, as the following result shows.

Proposition 4.1.

LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)≥12​LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T})\geq\frac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}.

The proof is simple: it shows that for any feasible solution 𝐱¯\bar{\bf x} to LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}, 𝐱¯/2\bar{\bf x}/2 is feasible for LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) (with 𝐧{\bf n} defined so that (P-Balance) holds).

Proof.

Let 𝐱¯\bar{\bf x} be feasible for LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}. Define 𝐱=𝐱¯/2{\bf x}=\bar{\bf x}/2, and define 𝐧{\bf n} to make (P-Balance) hold. Because 𝐱¯\bar{\bf x} satisfies (OMN-Supply), we must have ni≥λi/(2​μi)n_{i}\geq\lambda_{i}/(2\mu_{i}). Apply (5) to see that the right side of (P-Availability) is at least λj​(1−e−ρ⁡(S))/2\lambda_{j}(1-e^{-\rho(S)})/2. Because 𝐱¯\bar{\bf x} satisfies (OMN-Presence), the left side of (P-Availability) is at most λj​(1−e−ρ⁡(S))/2\lambda_{j}(1-e^{-\rho(S)})/2, so (P-Availability) holds. Thus, (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) is feasible for LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}), with objective value 12​∑ri​j​x¯i​j\frac{1}{2}\sum r_{ij}\bar{x}_{ij}. ∎

Therefore, if we can find a static priority policy whose long-run average reward is at least LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}), this policy also earns at least half of the omniscient benchmark. Identifying such a policy is the goal of Sections 4.2 and 4.3.

4.2 Identifying a Policy and Bounding Its Performance

In this subsection, we define what it means for a static priority policy π\pi to be consistent with a feasible solution (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). The first condition is that the policy should only make matches in ℳ\mathcal{M}, and should not make (i,j)(i,j) matches if xi​j=0x_{ij}=0. The second condition comes from examining the constraints (P-Availability). If (P-Availability) is tight for a particular SS and jj, then intuitively, the linear program matches arriving type-jj agents with types in SS as frequently as possible, so SS should be a prefix of the priority list ≻j\succ_{j}. This condition is also inspired by Lemma 3.2, which says that for any static priority policy and any prefix SS of ≻j\succ_{j}, the constraint (SP-Availability) — the analog of (P-Availability) — is tight.

To formalize our definition, for any feasible solution (𝐧,𝐱)({{\bf n}},{{\bf x}}) to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), we define

𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)={∅≠S⊆ℳj:(P-Availability) holds with equality}.\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x})=\{\emptyset\neq{}S\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}\ :\eqref{eq:availability-alg}\text{ holds with equality}\}. (7)
Definition 4.1 (Primal consistency).

A static priority policy π={≻j}j∈𝒯\pi=\{\succ_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}} is consistent with a feasible solution (𝐧,𝐱)({{\bf n}},{{\bf x}}) of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) if π\pi only makes matches in ℳ∩{(i,j):xi​j>0}\mathcal{M}\cap\{(i,j):x_{ij}>0\}, and 𝒫j(𝐧,𝐱)⊆Prefixes(≻j)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x})\subseteq\text{Prefixes}(\succ_{j}) for all j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T}.

There may not be a unique π\pi consistent with (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}). For example, suppose that for type jj, we have x1​j=x4​j=0x_{1j}=x_{4j}=0, and there are two tight constraints in (P-Availability), corresponding to the sets {2,3}\{2,3\} and {2,3,5}\{2,3,5\}. Then a consistent static priority policy could choose either 2≻j3≻j5≻j∅2\succ_{j}3\succ_{j}5\succ_{j}\emptyset or 3≻j2≻j5≻j∅3\succ_{j}2\succ_{j}5\succ_{j}\emptyset. A separate concern is that there might be no static priority policy consistent with (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}). We address this concern in Section 4.3; for now, we proceed assuming such a policy exists. With this assumption, we prove Proposition 4.2 in Section C.3 and explain the main idea here.

Proposition 4.2.

If (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({{\bf n}^{*}},{{\bf x}^{*}}) is an optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) and π\pi is a static priority policy consistent with (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({{\bf n}^{*}},{{\bf x}^{*}}), then V⁡(π)≥LPPOL​(ℳ)V(\pi)\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}).

Proof sketch.

The key fact used in the proof is that, by Lemma 3.3, (P-Availability) is a tightening of the constraint (SP-Availability) satisfied by static priority policies. As a result, the steady-state quantities (𝐧π,𝐱π)({\bf n}^{\pi},{\bf x}^{\pi}) of π\pi, defined in (3), are typically not feasible for LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). However, this alone does not imply that 𝐱π{\bf x}^{\pi} yields a higher objective value than 𝐱∗{\bf x}^{*}. Our proof shows that the “arrow” from 𝐱π{\bf x}^{\pi} to 𝐱∗{\bf x}^{*} “pierces” the feasible region (see Figure 5). This implies that (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}) can be expressed as a convex combination of (𝐧π,𝐱π)({\bf n}^{\pi},{\bf x}^{\pi}) and another feasible point (𝐧^,𝐱^)(\hat{{\bf n}},\hat{{\bf x}}). If we let 𝐫∘𝐱=∑(i,j)∈ℳri​j​xi​j\mathbf{r}\circ{\bf x}=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}}r_{ij}x_{ij} denote the objective value of 𝐱{\bf x}, then we have 𝐫∘𝐱^≤𝐫∘𝐱∗\mathbf{r}\circ\hat{{\bf x}}\leq\mathbf{r}\circ{\bf x}^{*} by optimality of (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}), so it follows that V⁡(π)=𝐫∘𝐱π≥𝐫∘𝐱∗=LPPOL​(ℳ)V(\pi)=\mathbf{r}\circ{\bf x}^{\pi}\geq\mathbf{r}\circ{\bf x}^{*}=\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). ∎

4.3 Finding a Suitable Solution

Sections 4.1 and 4.2 establish two main results. First, LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)≥12​LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T})\geq\frac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}. Second, if we take an optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) and let π\pi be any static priority policy consistent with this solution, then V⁡(π)≥LPPOL​(ℳ)V(\pi)\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Combining these, any static priority policy consistent with an optimal solution (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}) of LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) has long-run average reward at least 12​LPOMN≥12​OMN\frac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{OMN}.

Two barriers remain. First, and most importantly, we have not guaranteed that there exists a static priority policy consistent with (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}). In fact, such a policy might not exist.99 9 For example, let there be two types, with r11=r22=1r_{11}=r_{22}=1 and r12=r21=5r_{12}=r_{21}=5, with λ1=μ1=μ2=1\lambda_{1}=\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=1 and λ2=2\lambda_{2}=2. Then when solving LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}), the constraint for j=1j=1, S={1,2}S=\{1,2\} is tight, but x11=0x_{11}=0. It is impossible to simultaneously have {1,2}\{1,2\} be a prefix of ≻1\succ_{1} and to have (1,1)(1,1) matches be unacceptable. Second, if we care not only about the existence of a good policy but also about our ability to find it, then one might be concerned about solving the linear program, given that (P-Availability) consists of exponentially many constraints.

In this subsection, we show how to find a set of matches ℳ\mathcal{M} and an optimal solution (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({{\bf n}^{*}},{{\bf x}^{*}}) to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) such that the following hold:

  1. 1.

    there exists a static priority policy consistent with (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({{\bf n}^{*}},{{\bf x}^{*}}), and

  2. 2.

    LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}).

From Propositions 4.1 and 4.2, it follows that such a policy earns at least half of the omniscient benchmark. Also, we show that such a policy can be found in time polynomial in the input size.1010 10 For simplicity, we assume that 𝝀\bm{\lambda}, 𝝁\bm{\mu}, and 𝐫\mathbf{r} are rational, and we call |𝒯||\mathcal{T}| plus their encoding length the input size. We also treat the constants γS\gamma_{S}, which involve exponentials, as rational numbers of polynomial encoding length that can be computed exactly. We do not dwell on the details of the arithmetic and the bookkeeping of encoding lengths—both could be handled using standard methods. The polynomial-time claims of Sections 5 and 6 rely on the same convention.

We start by giving a name to solutions with which some static priority policy is consistent.

Definition 4.2 (Suitable solution).

A feasible solution (𝐧,𝐱)({{\bf n}},{{\bf x}}) of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) is suitable if there is a static priority policy π\pi that is consistent with it.

Examining Definition 4.1, there are two things that might prevent a consistent policy from existing. One is that it might be impossible to make each S∈𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}) a prefix of ≻j\succ_{j}. For example, if for a given jj, (P-Availability) is tight for both {1}\{1\} and {2}\{2\}, then no consistent policy exists: these sets cannot both be prefixes of ≻j\succ_{j} (11 and 22 cannot both be the highest-priority partner for jj). Similar issues arise if the tight sets are, for example, {1,3}\{1,3\} and {1,2,4}\{1,2,4\}. Our next lemma states that we do not need to worry about this concern: given any feasible solution (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), the sets in 𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}) are “nested”, meaning that for any two sets in this family, one contains the other.

A second concern that might prevent a consistent policy from existing is that there might be a j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T} and S∈𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}), that is, a set whose constraint (P-Availability) is tight, and yet xi​j=0x_{ij}=0 for some i∈Si\in S. This causes problems, as one condition of consistency is that SS should be a prefix of ≻j\succ_{j}, and a second condition is that ii should be unacceptable to jj. Lemma 4.3 establishes that this possibility is the only barrier that might prevent (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) from being suitable.

Lemma 4.3.

Let (𝐧,𝐱)({{\bf n}},{{\bf x}}) be any feasible solution to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Then for each j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T}, the set function

Ψj​(S)≜1γS​(λj​γS​∑i∈Sni−∑i∈Sxi​j)\Psi_{j}(S)\triangleq\frac{1}{\gamma_{S}}\left(\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}-\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij}\right)

is submodular. Moreover, if S,S′∈𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)S,S^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}), then either S⊆S′S\subseteq S^{\prime} or S′⊆SS^{\prime}\subseteq S. Consequently, a feasible solution (𝐧,𝐱)({{\bf n}},{{\bf x}}) of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) is suitable if and only if

xi​j>0for all ​j∈𝒯,S∈𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱), and ​i∈S.x_{ij}>0\quad\text{for all }j\in\mathcal{T},\ S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}),\text{ and }i\in S. (8)

Lemma 4.3, which we prove in Section C.3, establishes that (8) is necessary and sufficient for a consistent policy to exist. We now show how to find a choice of ℳ\mathcal{M} such that an optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) is suitable.

Recall that 𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}), defined in (7), consists of the sets for which (P-Availability) is tight. Thus, (8) says that if xi​jx_{ij} is involved in a tight constraint, then it should be positive. We can ensure that this condition is satisfied using the following algorithm. First solve LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}). Any (i,j)(i,j) such that xi​j=0x_{ij}=0 could potentially cause unsuitability, so remove these pairs from ℳ\mathcal{M} and re-solve LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Repeat until xi​j>0x_{ij}>0 for all (i,j)∈ℳ(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}, ensuring suitability of the solution by Lemma 4.3. Because the solution from each iteration is feasible for the next iteration, the optimal value never decreases throughout the procedure. We call this procedure pruning and formalize it in Algorithm 1 and Proposition 4.5.

Each iteration of this procedure solves a linear program of the form LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), which brings us back to the second barrier: LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has exponentially many availability constraints. These constraints, however, admit an efficient separation oracle. The key is the submodularity established in Lemma 4.3. For a nonnegative candidate solution (𝐧^,𝐱^)(\hat{{\bf n}},\hat{{\bf x}}), the availability constraints (P-Availability) for arrivals of type jj hold if and only if Ψj​(S)≥0\Psi_{j}(S)\geq 0 for every nonempty subset S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}. Submodular minimization can therefore either certify these constraints or identify a violated one (Schrijver 2000). Together with directly checking the other constraints, this gives an exact polynomial-time separation oracle for LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). We can then use the standard equivalence of separation and optimization (Grötschel et al. 1988), which yields a polynomial-time algorithm based on the ellipsoid method for computing an exact optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). We do not dwell on the details of the arithmetic (see footnote 10). Formally, we have the following proposition.

Proposition 4.4.

For every ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, an optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) can be computed in time polynomial in the input size.

The proof is deferred to Section C.3.

Proposition 4.5.

Algorithm 1 returns a set ℳ\mathcal{M} such that LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}), as well as a suitable optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Furthermore, Algorithm 1 runs in time polynomial in the input size.

Proof.
