Every iteration except the last removes at least one of the |𝒯|2|\mathcal{T}|^{2} pairs, so the process stops after at most |𝒯|2+1|\mathcal{T}|^{2}+1 iterations, and each iteration solves one linear program, which takes polynomial time by Proposition 4.4.

When this process stops, by definition xi​jk>0x^{k}_{ij}>0 for each (i,j)∈ℳ(k)(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{(k)}, so by Lemma 4.3, the solution must be suitable. To see that the RkR_{k} form a nondecreasing sequence, notice that the solution (𝐧k,𝐱k)({\bf n}^{k},{\bf x}^{k}) of LPPOL​(ℳ(k−1))\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}^{(k-1)}) is also feasible for LPPOL​(ℳ(k))\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}^{(k)}), since ℳj(k)⊆ℳj(k−1)\mathcal{M}^{(k)}_{j}\subseteq\mathcal{M}^{(k-1)}_{j} for every jj and therefore (P-Availability) encodes fewer constraints. (Technically, LPPOL​(ℳ(k))\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}^{(k)}) involves fewer decision variables; we simply ignore the values xi​jkx_{ij}^{k} for which (i,j)∉ℳ(k)(i,j)\notin\mathcal{M}^{(k)}.) Furthermore, this feasible solution of LPPOL​(ℳ(k))\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}^{(k)}) still has value RkR_{k}, since by definition xi​jk=0x_{ij}^{k}=0 for each (i,j)∈ℳ(k−1)∖ℳ(k)(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}^{(k-1)}\setminus\mathcal{M}^{(k)}. Hence Rk+1≥RkR_{k+1}\geq R_{k}, and the value of the returned program is at least R1=LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)R_{1}=\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}). ∎

Let (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) be the solution returned by Algorithm 1. A static priority policy consistent with (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) can also be computed in polynomial time. Fix j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T}, and note that Ψj​(∅)=0\Psi_{j}(\emptyset)=0 and, by feasibility, Ψj​(S)≥0\Psi_{j}(S)\geq 0 for every nonempty S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}. Thus, a type i∈ℳji\in\mathcal{M}_{j} belongs to some set in 𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}) if and only if the minimum of Ψj\Psi_{j} over the sets S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j} that contain ii is zero, and some set in 𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}) contains ii but not i′i^{\prime} if and only if the minimum of Ψj\Psi_{j} over the sets S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j} that contain ii but not i′i^{\prime} is zero. Each of these minimizations is a submodular minimization, which takes polynomial time (Schrijver 2000). Since the sets in 𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}) are nested, we can then rank as acceptable exactly the types that belong to some set in 𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}), with i≻ji′i\succ_{j}i^{\prime} whenever some set in 𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}) contains ii but not i′i^{\prime} and with the remaining ties broken arbitrarily. As in the proof of Lemma 4.3, since (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) satisfies (8), the resulting static priority policy is consistent with (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}).

5 Dual Approach

The primal approach of Section 4 identifies a static priority policy by solving a linear program and reading the priorities off its tight constraints. We now describe a second, dual-based way to identify such policies and certify their reward. This section focuses on the specific class of value-based static priority policies that were introduced earlier. As a reminder, such a policy gives each type a value that captures the opportunity cost of matching an agent of that type, and prioritizes matches by their score: the reward minus the values of the two matched types. Since the values will serve as dual variables (as we formalize shortly), the scores can be interpreted as dual-adjusted rewards.

As in Section 4, it is convenient to fix a set of matches ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T} outside of which the policy never matches. Formally, we define such restricted value-based policies, which are described by one number viv_{i} per type ii together with the set ℳ\mathcal{M}, as follows.

Definition 5.1 (Dual consistency).

Given a vector of values 𝐯∈ℝ𝒯\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{T}} and a set of matches ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, we say a static priority policy π={≻j}j∈𝒯\pi=\{\succ_{j}\}_{j\in\mathcal{T}} is consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯\mathbf{v} if it satisfies the following:

  • •

    The set of acceptable matches ℳ(π)={(i,j):i≻j∅}\mathcal{M}(\pi)=\{(i,j):i\succ_{j}\emptyset\} is a subset of ℳ∩{(i,j):ri​j−vi−vj≥0}\mathcal{M}\cap{}\{(i,j):r_{ij}-v_{i}-v_{j}\geq 0\}.

  • •

    If (i,j)∈ℳ(i,j)\in\mathcal{M} and ri​j−vi−vj>0r_{ij}-v_{i}-v_{j}>0, then i≻j∅i\succ_{j}\emptyset.

  • •

    If (i,j),(i′,j)∈ℳ(i,j),(i^{\prime},j)\in\mathcal{M} and ri​j−vi−vj>ri′​j−vi′−vj≥0r_{ij}-v_{i}-v_{j}>r_{i^{\prime}j}-v_{i^{\prime}}-v_{j}\geq 0, then i≻ji′i\succ_{j}i^{\prime}.

When ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T} we simply say that π\pi is consistent with 𝐯\mathbf{v}.

In words, a value-based policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯\mathbf{v} makes only matches in ℳ\mathcal{M} with nonnegative score ri​j−vi−vjr_{ij}-v_{i}-v_{j}, makes every match in ℳ\mathcal{M} with positive score acceptable, and ranks the acceptable partners of each arriving type in decreasing order of score (i.e., of dual-adjusted reward). Such a policy always exists, although it might not be unique: ties between equal scores may be broken arbitrarily, and a match with score exactly zero may be either acceptable or unacceptable.

In fact, the unrestricted case ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T} suffices for the guarantee of this section. Therefore, our main analysis in this section sets ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, and shows how to find values 𝐯\mathbf{v} that simultaneously (i) certify a lower bound on the long-run average reward of every policy consistent with them, and (ii) make this lower bound at least half of the omniscient benchmark. A general set ℳ\mathcal{M} is needed only in Section 5.4 and later in Section 6, where we connect the policies of this section with those of Section 4, which make matches only within the set ℳ\mathcal{M} returned by Algorithm 1.

5.1 Value-Based Certificates

For the first goal, we begin with a linear program, inspired by Lemma 3.3, that provides a lower bound on the long-run average reward of an arbitrary static priority policy π\pi; in particular, π\pi need not be value-based. As before, ℳ(π)={(i,j):i≻j∅}\mathcal{M}(\pi)=\{(i,j):i\succ_{j}\emptyset\} denotes its set of acceptable matches, and 𝒫j​(π)\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi) denotes the collection of prefixes of ≻j\succ_{j} (Definition 3.1). We then introduce the following LP:

This LP is similar in spirit to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), with two important differences. First, its objective and constraints depend on π\pi, so ( π -Availability) consists of at most |𝒯|2|\mathcal{T}|^{2} constraints, rather than one constraint for each arriving type jj and nonempty set S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}. Second, it minimizes rather than maximizes its objective, its availability constraints are reversed, and its balance constraints are inequalities (≥\geq) rather than equalities. As a result, it provides a lower bound on V⁡(π)V(\pi): the steady-state quantities (𝐧π,𝐱π)({\bf n}^{\pi},{\bf x}^{\pi}) defined in (3) form a feasible solution of LPLB​(π){\textup{LP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi) with objective value ∑(i,j)∈ℳ⁡(π)ri​j​xi​jπ=V⁡(π)\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}(\pi)}r_{ij}x_{ij}^{\pi}=V(\pi). Indeed, Lemma 3.2 shows that these quantities satisfy ( π -Balance) with equality, while Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 together imply that, for every j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T} and prefix S∈𝒫j​(π)S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi),

∑i∈Sxi​jπ=λj​ℙ​(∑i∈SNiπ>0)≥λj​γS​∑i∈Sniπ,\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij}^{\pi}=\lambda_{j}\mathbb{P}\!\left(\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi}>0\right)\geq\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}^{\pi},

which establishes ( π -Availability).

We now take the dual of LPLB​(π){\textup{LP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi), associating a dual variable viv_{i} with the constraint ( π -Balance) of type ii and a dual variable zS​jz_{Sj} with the constraint ( π -Availability) of type jj and prefix SS. This yields the following maximization linear program:

The notation viv_{i} for the dual variable of the constraint ( π -Balance) of type ii is deliberate: we will use a particular (not necessarily optimal) choice of these dual variables as the values of a value-based policy. With this viewpoint, each constraint (9) states that the values of the two agents consumed by an acceptable match, together with the weights zS​jz_{Sj} of the prefixes containing the waiting partner, do not exceed the reward of the match. Also, each constraint (10) states that the rate μi​vi\mu_{i}v_{i} at which value is lost to abandonment per waiting type-ii agent does not exceed a pessimistic estimate of the rate at which the agent’s availability generates surplus for arriving agents, as we explain next.

Fix an arriving type jj, list its acceptable partners as i1≻j⋯≻jimi_{1}\succ_{j}\cdots\succ_{j}i_{m}, and let Pk={i1,…,ik}P_{k}=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}. When the constraints (9) of type jj hold with equality, as they will for the values we construct, the score rik​j−vik−vjr_{i_{k}j}-v_{i_{k}}-v_{j} equals ∑ℓ≥kzPℓ​j\sum_{\ell\geq k}z_{P_{\ell}j}, the total weight of the prefixes that contain iki_{k}. As a result, this total weight accounts for the surplus of the match, that is, the part of its reward that exceeds the values of the two matched agents, which is its score rik​j−vik−vjr_{i_{k}j}-v_{i_{k}}-v_{j}. Equivalently, zPk​jz_{P_{k}j} is the drop in score from the kk-th to the (k+1)(k+1)-th type on the list, where the score after the last type is taken to be zero; as a result, zPℓ​jz_{P_{\ell}j} can be interpreted as the contribution of the prefix PℓP_{\ell} to the surplus generated by each match of an arriving type-jj agent with a partner in PℓP_{\ell}. By ( π -Availability), such matches occur at a rate of at least λj​γPℓ​∑i∈Pℓniπ\lambda_{j}\gamma_{P_{\ell}}\sum_{i\in P_{\ell}}n^{\pi}_{i}. Intuitively speaking, spreading this contribution evenly over the waiting agents in PℓP_{\ell} credits each of them with surplus at rate λj​γPℓ​zPℓ​j\lambda_{j}\gamma_{P_{\ell}}z_{P_{\ell}j}. Summing over arriving types and prefixes that contain type ii, each waiting type-ii agent is credited with surplus at rate ∑j∑S∈𝒫j​(π)λj​γS​zS​j​𝟏​(i∈S)\sum_{j}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi)}\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}z_{Sj}\mathbf{1}(i\in S), which is the right side of (10).

Weak duality now provides conditions under which a vector of values serves as a lower-bound certificate for the long-run average reward of a given static priority policy.

Proposition 5.1.

Let π\pi be a static priority policy and let (𝐯,𝐳)(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{z}) be feasible for DLPLB​(π)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{LB}}(\pi). Then

V⁡(π)≥∑i∈𝒯λi​vi.V(\pi)\geq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v_{i}.
Proof.

Since the primal program LPLB​(π){\textup{LP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi) lower-bounds the long-run average reward V⁡(π)V(\pi) of policy π\pi, weak duality gives V⁡(π)≥LPLB​(π)≥∑i∈𝒯λi​viV(\pi)\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{LB}}(\pi)\geq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v_{i}, as desired. ∎

In summary, Proposition 5.1 states that nonnegative values 𝐯\mathbf{v} provide the desired certificate for a policy π\pi if there exist nonnegative prefix weights 𝐳\mathbf{z} such that the pair (𝐯,𝐳)(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{z}) satisfies (9) and (10). We next look for such a certificate, together with its corresponding static priority policy, that also provides a bound on the omniscient benchmark.

5.2 Bounding the Omniscient Benchmark via Values

The second objective of this section is to find values 𝐯\mathbf{v}, together with prefix weights 𝐳\mathbf{z}, that “cover” the omniscient benchmark, meaning that ∑iλi​vi\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i} bounds it from above (up to a multiplicative factor). Since LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} upper-bounds the omniscient benchmark (Proposition 2.3), it is natural to look for such a bound through the dual of LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}. As it turns out, the key is to reverse the inequalities in (9) and (10). We formalize this claim in the following proposition, whose proof relates these reversed inequalities to the objective and constraints of the dual of LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}. We sketch the proof below and defer the full proof to Section C.4.1.

Proposition 5.2.

Fix a static priority policy π\pi. Suppose that (vi)i∈𝒯(v_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{T}} and (zS​j)j∈𝒯,S∈𝒫j​(π)(z_{Sj})_{j\in\mathcal{T},\,S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi)} satisfy vi,zS​j≥0v_{i},z_{Sj}\geq 0 and

vi+vj+∑S∈𝒫j​(π)zS​j​𝟏​(i∈S)≥ri​j\displaystyle v_{i}+v_{j}+\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi)}z_{Sj}\mathbf{1}(i\in S)\geq r_{ij} ∀i,j∈𝒯,\displaystyle\forall i,j\in\mathcal{T}, (11)
μi​vi≥∑j∈𝒯∑S∈𝒫j​(π)λj​γS​zS​j​𝟏​(i∈S)\displaystyle\mu_{i}v_{i}\geq\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi)}\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}z_{Sj}\mathbf{1}(i\in S) ∀i∈𝒯.\displaystyle\forall i\in\mathcal{T}. (12)

Then ∑iλi​vi≥12​LPOMN\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}.

Proof sketch.

Extending the prefix weights by zero to all subsets of 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the reversed constraints (11) say precisely that (𝐯,𝐳)(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{z}) is feasible for the dual of LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}, whose objective is

∑i∈𝒯λi​vi+∑j∈𝒯∑S⊆𝒯λj​(1−e−ρ⁡(S))​zS​j.\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v_{i}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{j}(1-e^{-\rho(S)})z_{Sj}.

Multiplying the constraints (12) by λi/μi\lambda_{i}/\mu_{i} and summing over ii shows that this objective is at most 2​∑iλi​vi2\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}. Weak duality then gives LPOMN≤2​∑iλi​vi\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}\leq 2\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}.1111 11 This is a dual form of Proposition 4.1, which establishes an analogous bound between LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} and LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}). See also Section 6.1, which relates the dual of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) to these conditions. ∎

5.3 Satisfying Both Requirements via a Fixed Point

Propositions 5.1 and 5.2 show that a static priority policy π\pi earns at least 12​LPOMN\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}, and hence at least half of the omniscient benchmark, whenever the policy π\pi, the values 𝐯\mathbf{v}, and the prefix weights 𝐳\mathbf{z} satisfy (9), (10), (11), and (12). These four sets of conditions are equivalent to the following:

vi+vj+∑S∈𝒫j​(π)zS​j​𝟏​(i∈S)\displaystyle v_{i}+v_{j}+\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi)}z_{Sj}\mathbf{1}(i\in S) =ri​j\displaystyle=r_{ij} ∀(i,j)∈ℳ⁡(π),\displaystyle\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}(\pi), (13)
μi​vi\displaystyle\mu_{i}v_{i} =∑j∑S∈𝒫j​(π)λj​γS​zS​j​𝟏​(i∈S)\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\sum_{S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi)}\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}z_{Sj}\mathbf{1}(i\in S) ∀i∈𝒯,\displaystyle\forall i\in\mathcal{T}, (14)
vi+vj\displaystyle v_{i}+v_{j} ≥ri​j\displaystyle\geq r_{ij} ∀(i,j)∉ℳ⁡(π),\displaystyle\forall(i,j)\notin\mathcal{M}(\pi), (15)
zS​j\displaystyle z_{Sj} ≥0\displaystyle\geq 0 ∀j∈𝒯,S∈𝒫j​(π).\displaystyle\forall j\in\mathcal{T},\ S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi). (16)

Specifically, (9) and (11) are equivalent to (13) and (15), while (10) and (12) are equivalent to (14). The nonnegativity of 𝐯\mathbf{v} is implied by (14) and (16).

How can we find a policy π\pi, values 𝐯\mathbf{v}, and prefix weights 𝐳\mathbf{z} that satisfy these conditions? The conditions themselves point the way. Fix an arriving type jj. Recall from an earlier discussion in Section 5.1 that by (13) and (16), the scores ri​j−vi−vjr_{ij}-v_{i}-v_{j} of its acceptable partners are nonnegative and nonincreasing along ≻j\succ_{j}, and the weight of each prefix is the drop in score from one type on the list to the next. By (15), every match with a positive score is acceptable. Thus, once the values are fixed, the prefix weights are determined, and so are the priority lists, up to ties and zero-score matches. The conditions (14) then become a system of equations in the values alone.

We now write this system of equations explicitly for a general set of allowed matches ℳ\mathcal{M}—as we need it later in Sections 5.4 and 6. Fix a set of matches ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, recall that ℳj={i:(i,j)∈ℳ}\mathcal{M}_{j}=\{i:(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}\}, and for a vector of values 𝐯\mathbf{v} write ui​j​(𝐯)=(ri​j−vi−vj)+u_{ij}(\mathbf{v})=(r_{ij}-v_{i}-v_{j})^{+} for the residual score of an (i,j)(i,j) match, that is, the positive part of its score. For an arriving type jj and a nonempty set S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}, let

ZS​jℳ​(𝐯)≜(mini∈S⁡ui​j​(𝐯)−maxi∈ℳj∖S⁡ui​j​(𝐯))+,Z^{\mathcal{M}}_{Sj}(\mathbf{v})\triangleq\left(\min_{i\in S}u_{ij}(\mathbf{v})-\max_{i\in\mathcal{M}_{j}\setminus S}u_{ij}(\mathbf{v})\right)^{+}, (17)

where the maximum or minimum over the empty set is taken to be zero, and for every i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T} let

Fiℳ​(𝐯)≜1μi​∑j∈𝒯λj​∑S⊆ℳjγS​ZS​jℳ​(𝐯)​𝟏​(i∈S).F^{\mathcal{M}}_{i}(\mathbf{v})\triangleq\frac{1}{\mu_{i}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{j}\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}}\gamma_{S}Z^{\mathcal{M}}_{Sj}(\mathbf{v})\mathbf{1}(i\in S). (18)

The weight ZS​jℳ​(𝐯)Z^{\mathcal{M}}_{Sj}(\mathbf{v}) is positive only if every type in SS has a positive score that is strictly larger than the score of every type in ℳj∖S\mathcal{M}_{j}\setminus S; it is then the gap between the smallest score inside SS and the largest score outside SS, where negative scores are replaced by zero. The sets carrying positive weight for type jj are therefore nested: each is a prefix of the list of types in ℳj\mathcal{M}_{j} ranked in decreasing order of the residual scores ui​j​(𝐯)u_{ij}(\mathbf{v}). Moreover, the weights telescope along this chain:

∑S⊆ℳjZS​jℳ​(𝐯)​ 1​(i∈S)=ui​j​(𝐯)∀(i,j)∈ℳ.\sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}}Z^{\mathcal{M}}_{Sj}(\mathbf{v})\,\mathbf{1}(i\in S)=u_{ij}(\mathbf{v})\qquad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}. (19)

We write 𝐙ℳ​(𝐯)=(ZS​jℳ​(𝐯))j,S\mathbf{Z}^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{v})=(Z^{\mathcal{M}}_{Sj}(\mathbf{v}))_{j,S} for the vector of these weights. When ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T} we drop the superscript and write ZS​j​(𝐯)Z_{Sj}(\mathbf{v}) and Fi​(𝐯)F_{i}(\mathbf{v}).

Returning to the unrestricted case ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, the following proposition, whose proof is deferred to Section C.4.2, confirms that finding a policy π\pi, values 𝐯\mathbf{v}, and prefix weights 𝐳\mathbf{z} that satisfy (13)–(16) reduces to finding a fixed point of the map 𝐅\mathbf{F}.

Proposition 5.3.

A vector 𝐯≥0\mathbf{v}\geq 0 admits a static priority policy π\pi and weights 𝐳\mathbf{z} satisfying (13)–(16) only if 𝐅⁡(𝐯)=𝐯\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{v}. Conversely, if 𝐅⁡(𝐯)=𝐯\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{v}, then every static priority policy π\pi consistent with 𝐯\mathbf{v} (Definition 5.1), together with the weights zS​j=ZS​j​(𝐯)z_{Sj}=Z_{Sj}(\mathbf{v}) for j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T} and S∈𝒫j​(π)S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi), satisfies (13)–(16).

The fixed-point equation 𝐅⁡(𝐯)=𝐯\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{v} has an intuitive economic interpretation. For each type ii, we can write it as μi​vi=μi​Fi​(𝐯)\mu_{i}v_{i}=\mu_{i}F_{i}(\mathbf{v}). Its left side is the rate at which value is lost to abandonment per waiting type-ii agent, and its right side is the pessimistic estimate, discussed earlier, of the rate at which that agent’s availability generates surplus for arrivals of all types. A fixed point makes these two rates equal and, in this sense, yields a “balanced” vector of values—cf. the balanced thresholds and prices used in prophet inequalities (Kleinberg and Weinberg 2019, Dütting et al. 2020).

Taken together, these results show that the existence of a fixed point of 𝐅\mathbf{F} suffices for the guarantee of 12\tfrac{1}{2} in this section. In fact, it is straightforward to use Brouwer’s theorem (Brouwer 1911) to show the existence. We go a step further: for every set of matches ℳ\mathcal{M}, the fixed point of the restricted map 𝐅ℳ\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}} is unique and can be computed in polynomial time. (See footnote 10 for our convention about arithmetic representations). We sketch the proof below and defer the full proof to Section C.4.2. Notably, uniqueness is used in Sections 5.4 and 6. Moreover, Section 6 also gives an alternative, LP-based way to compute the restricted fixed point for a broad class of sets ℳ\mathcal{M} and shows that it is sufficient for our purpose of obtaining 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive value-based policies.

Proposition 5.4.

For every set of matches ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, the map 𝐅ℳ\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}} has a unique fixed point in ℝ𝒯\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{T}}, which we call the restricted fixed point and denote by 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}. Moreover, 𝐯ℳ≥0\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}\geq 0, and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} can be computed in time polynomial in the input size.

Proof sketch.

Existence, uniqueness, and computation all rely on a one-sided Lipschitz bound, which we prove in Lemma C.2: with ⟨𝐚,𝐛⟩𝝀=∑iλi​ai​bi\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}\rangle_{\bm{\lambda}}=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}a_{i}b_{i} and ‖𝐚‖𝝀=⟨𝐚,𝐚⟩𝝀1/2\|\mathbf{a}\|_{\bm{\lambda}}=\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{a}\rangle_{\bm{\lambda}}^{1/2},

⟨𝐅ℳ​(𝐯)−𝐅ℳ​(𝐰),𝐯−𝐰⟩𝝀≤12​‖𝐯−𝐰‖𝝀2for all ​𝐯,𝐰∈ℝ𝒯.\big\langle\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{v})-\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{w}),\,\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{w}\big\rangle_{\bm{\lambda}}\;\leq\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,\|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{w}\|_{\bm{\lambda}}^{2}\qquad\text{for all }\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{T}}. (20)

Intuitively, raising the value of a type lowers the surplus credited to its availability, and in the λ\lambda-weighted inner product this effect outweighs the surplus that shifts to other types. The map 𝐅ℳ\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}} itself need not be a contraction, but (20) and a Lipschitz bound imply that the damped map 𝐯↦(1−θ)​𝐯+θ​𝐅ℳ​(𝐯)\mathbf{v}\mapsto(1-\theta)\mathbf{v}+\theta\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{v}), which has the same fixed points, is a contraction with respect to ∥⋅∥𝝀\|\cdot\|_{\bm{\lambda}} for small enough θ>0\theta>0. Banach’s fixed-point theorem then gives existence and uniqueness, and the fixed point is nonnegative because 𝐅ℳ\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}} takes nonnegative values. For the computation, ellipsoid methods for fixed points of contractions (Sikorski et al. 1993, Daskalakis et al. 2026) approximate the fixed point to within any accuracy ε\varepsilon in time polynomial in the input size and log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon), using only evaluations of 𝐅ℳ\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}}, each of which amounts to sorting scores. Since 𝐅ℳ\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}} is piecewise affine, a sufficiently accurate approximation determines the fixed point exactly. ∎

Putting all the pieces together, we can prove the following main result of this section.

Theorem 5.5.

There exists a vector of values 𝐯≥0\mathbf{v}\geq 0 such that for any static priority policy π\pi consistent with 𝐯\mathbf{v}, V⁡(π)≥12​LPOMNV(\pi)\geq\frac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}. Moreover, such a vector, and a static priority policy consistent with it, can be computed in time polynomial in the input size.

Proof.

Let 𝐯=𝐯𝒯×𝒯\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}} be the fixed point of 𝐅\mathbf{F} given by Proposition 5.4, and let π\pi be any static priority policy consistent with 𝐯\mathbf{v}. By Proposition 5.3, the weights zS​j=ZS​j​(𝐯)z_{Sj}=Z_{Sj}(\mathbf{v}) on the prefixes of π\pi complete a triple (π,𝐯,𝐳)(\pi,\mathbf{v},\mathbf{z}) satisfying (13)–(16). Hence (𝐯,𝐳)(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{z}) is feasible for DLPLB​(π){\textup{DLP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi), and Proposition 5.1 gives V⁡(π)≥∑iλi​viV(\pi)\geq\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}, while (𝐯,𝐳)(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{z}) satisfies the conditions of Proposition 5.2, which gives ∑iλi​vi≥12​LPOMN\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}. Combining the two inequalities proves the desired statement. Finally, by Proposition 5.4, 𝐯𝒯×𝒯\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}} can be computed in polynomial time, and a policy consistent with it is obtained by ranking, for each arriving type, its partners with positive scores in decreasing order of score. ∎

5.4 Discussion: A Family of Optimally Competitive Value-based Policies

The policy in Section 4 makes matches only within a set ℳ\mathcal{M} carefully selected by Algorithm 1. In contrast, the value-based policy in Theorem 5.5 is defined on the unrestricted set 𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, although Definition 5.1 and the map 𝐅ℳ\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}} allow for a general set ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}. Moreover, Proposition 5.4 establishes the existence of a unique fixed point not only for 𝐅\mathbf{F}, but also for every restricted map 𝐅ℳ\mathbf{F}^{\mathcal{M}}. This raises the question of whether we can generalize the machinery developed in this section to design a broader class of value-based policies, each of which is restricted to a properly chosen set ℳ\mathcal{M} and remains 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive against the omniscient benchmark.1212 12 An arbitrary set ℳ\mathcal{M} need not preserve this guarantee; for example, ℳ=∅\mathcal{M}=\emptyset precludes all matches.

As a natural step, consider computing the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} and running a static priority policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}. As we show next, we can use the values 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} to certify the reward of this policy, in a manner similar to the value lower-bound certificate in Section 5.1 (Proposition 5.1).

Lemma 5.6.

Let ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, and let π\pi be a static priority policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}. Then:

V⁡(π)≥∑i∈𝒯λi​viℳ.V(\pi)\geq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v^{\mathcal{M}}_{i}.

We prove this lemma in Section C.4.3 using weak duality: the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}, together with its associated weights zS​j=ZS​jℳ​(𝐯ℳ),∀j∈𝒯,S∈𝒫j​(π)z_{Sj}=Z^{\mathcal{M}}_{Sj}(\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}})~,~\forall j\in\mathcal{T},\ S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}(\pi), is feasible for DLPLB​(π)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{LB}}(\pi) and Proposition 5.1 gives the desired bound.

Restricting to ℳ\mathcal{M} preserves the lower-bound certificate for the policy but does not necessarily provide a comparison with the omniscient benchmark. To obtain this comparison, one could try applying Proposition 5.2 directly and impose reversed constraints (11) and (12) on 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}. However, as we show in Section C.4.3, this would result in exactly the same fixed point 𝐯𝒯×𝒯\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}}, and the same policy as in Theorem 5.5. A restriction that changes the fixed point (and the policy) requires a different argument to compare the policy’s lower-bound certificate with the omniscient benchmark.

The natural yardstick for this new comparison is the program LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) from Section 4, since LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)≥12​LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T})\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} by Proposition 4.1. Our next lemma shows that, for every ℳ\mathcal{M}, the reward certified by the restricted fixed point is at least the value of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}).

Lemma 5.7.

For every ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, we have ∑i∈𝒯λi​viℳ≥LPPOL​(ℳ)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v^{\mathcal{M}}_{i}\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}).

We prove this lemma in Section C.4.3 also using weak duality: the restricted fixed point, together with its associated weights, is feasible for the dual of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Given this result, for a policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} to earn at least half of the omniscient benchmark, it suffices that

LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) (21)

Putting everything together suggests a recipe: let ℳ\mathcal{M} be any set such that (21) holds, and let π\pi be any static priority policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}. Lemma 5.6 bounds the policy’s reward from below by ∑i∈𝒯λi​viℳ\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v^{\mathcal{M}}_{i}, while Lemma 5.7 shows that this certified value is at least LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Combining these inequalities with (21) and the benchmark bounds in Propositions 4.1 and 2.3 gives

V⁡(π)≥∑i∈𝒯λi​viℳ≥LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)≥12​LPOMN≥12​OMN.V(\pi)\;\geq\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v^{\mathcal{M}}_{i}\;\geq\;\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\;\geq\;\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T})\;\geq\;\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}}\;\geq\;\tfrac{1}{2}\textup{OMN}. (22)

Thus, every such policy is 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive against the omniscient benchmark. This more general approach, therefore, yields a larger class of 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive value-based static priority policies, whose priorities are based on restricted fixed points 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} for properly chosen sets ℳ\mathcal{M}, namely, those satisfying (21). This class contains the unrestricted value-based policies of Theorem 5.5, which correspond to ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}. As another example, note that (21) is true for the pruned set ℳ\mathcal{M} returned by Algorithm 1 (Proposition 4.5). Interestingly, the resulting value-based policy coincides with the primal policy from Section 4, which we will show in the next section.

6 Primal Meets Dual: Connections and Computations

Sections 4 and 5 develop two seemingly different approaches to constructing a static priority policy that earns at least half of the omniscient benchmark. In Section 4, the priority lists are read from the tight availability constraints of a suitable optimal solution to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), and the policy’s reward is certified by the piercing argument of Proposition 4.2. In Section 5, the priority lists are determined by a vector of values satisfying the fixed-point equation for 𝐅\mathbf{F}, and the reward is certified through the dual programs DLPLB​(π){\textup{DLP}^{\textup{LB}}}(\pi). The two approaches thus appear to rely on different objects: tight LP constraints in one case and fixed-point values in the other. In this section, we show that the two routes lead to the same place and that these objects are directly connected: the primal priorities already encode a vector of restricted fixed-point values.

The key to this connection is the linear programming dual of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), which we state in Section 6.1. Here is how this section is organized to provide details of this connection:

  1. (i)

    We first show in Section 6.1 that if ℳ\mathcal{M} is properly selected so that LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) admits a suitable optimal solution (as defined in Section 4), then the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}, together with its associated weights, is an optimal solution to the dual of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Moreover, this optimal dual solution is unique, and solving the dual of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) recovers 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}.

  2. (ii)

    We then show in Section 6.2 that the static priority policy of Section 4 is a value-based policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and these same values 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}. In short, the primal-based algorithm in Section 4 is, in fact, a dual-based algorithm in disguise.

We highlight that this connection works in both directions: it provides a value-based interpretation of the primal priorities and, conversely, turns LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) and its dual into an LP-based alternative to Proposition 5.4 for computing the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} whenever LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a suitable optimal solution. For the set returned by Algorithm 1, this yields a 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive polynomial-time value-based policy that may differ from the unrestricted policy in Section 5. We provide more details on the polynomial-time computation in Section 6.3. All proofs in this section, except the short proof of Theorem 6.4, are deferred to Section C.5.

6.1 Suitability and Recovering the Restricted Fixed Point via LP

By Proposition 5.4, the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} can be computed in polynomial time by solving the fixed-point equation directly. We now present an alternative based on linear programming that computes 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} for a broad class of sets ℳ\mathcal{M}, including the set returned by Algorithm 1.

Fix a set of matches ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}. Now consider the dual of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) by associating a dual variable viv_{i} with the balance constraint (P-Balance) for each type ii, and a dual variable zS​jz_{Sj} with the availability constraint (P-Availability) for each type jj and nonempty set S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}:1313 13 Every feasible solution to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) satisfies ni>0n_{i}>0 for all i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T}; see the proof of Lemma 4.3. Complementary slackness therefore implies that the dual constraints (24) hold with equality at every optimal solution to DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}).

Importantly, these constraints have the same form as those of DLPLB​(π)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{LB}}(\pi), but with the inequalities reversed. The constraints (23) are imposed on the pairs in ℳ\mathcal{M} rather than on the acceptable pairs of a policy, and the weights are assigned to all nonempty subsets of ℳj\mathcal{M}_{j} rather than only to prefixes. The direction of the inequalities reflects the direction of the certificate: by weak duality, every feasible solution to DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) satisfies ∑iλi​vi≥LPPOL​(ℳ)\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), whereas every feasible solution to DLPLB​(π)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{LB}}(\pi) satisfies ∑iλi​vi≤V⁡(π)\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}v_{i}\leq V(\pi).

The restricted fixed point, together with its associated weights, satisfies both sets of constraints at once: it is feasible for DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) (see the proof of Lemma 5.7), and, with its weights restricted to the prefixes of π\pi, it is feasible for DLPLB​(π)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{LB}}(\pi) for every policy π\pi consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} (see the proof of Lemma 5.6). Moreover, the constraints (23) are tight on every pair in ℳ\mathcal{M} with nonnegative score. One might therefore hope to recover 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} by solving DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). However, this need not work for an arbitrary ℳ\mathcal{M}: Example D.1 in Appendix D exhibits an instance with ℳ=𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T} in which the optimal dual values are not a fixed point, and the value-based policy constructed from them earns less than LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}).

Despite the above negative result, we show that the restricted fixed point and its associated weights form the unique optimal solution to DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) if and only if LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a suitable optimal solution in the sense of Section 4.3. Thus, the exact same condition that allows us to read a policy from the primal solution in Section 4 also ensures that solving the dual recovers 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} in Section 5.

Proposition 6.1.

Let ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T} be a set of matches. The following statements are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a suitable optimal solution.

  2. 2.

    Every optimal solution (𝐯∗,𝐳∗)(\mathbf{v}^{*},\mathbf{z}^{*}) to DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) satisfies 𝐳∗=𝐙ℳ​(𝐯∗)\mathbf{z}^{*}=\mathbf{Z}^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{v}^{*}).

Moreover, when these conditions hold, DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a unique optimal solution, consisting of the restricted fixed point and its associated weights:

(𝐯∗,𝐳∗)=(𝐯ℳ,𝐙ℳ​(𝐯ℳ)).(\mathbf{v}^{*},\mathbf{z}^{*})=\big(\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}},\mathbf{Z}^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}})\big).

In particular,

LPPOL​(ℳ)=DLPPOL​(ℳ)=∑i∈𝒯λi​viℳ.\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})=\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\lambda_{i}v^{\mathcal{M}}_{i}.

At a high level, the proof of this proposition is basically an exercise in complementary slackness and linear programming duality, and is deferred to Section C.5.1.

6.2 The Primal Policy Is a Value-Based Policy

We now return to the policy we constructed in Section 4 via the primal approach. Given a suitable optimal solution (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}) to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), consider any static priority policy consistent with it in the sense of Definition 4.1. Such a policy makes only matches in ℳ\mathcal{M} with xi​j∗>0x^{*}_{ij}>0, and every tight set S∈𝒫j​(𝐧∗,𝐱∗)S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}) is a prefix of ≻j\succ_{j}. The following result shows that this policy is consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and the dual values 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}.

Proposition 6.2.

Let ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, and let (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}) be a suitable optimal solution to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Then every static priority policy consistent with (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}) is also consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}.

Proof sketch.

The full proof of the proposition is deferred to Section C.5.2, and here we sketch the main ideas. The proposition again follows from complementary slackness, applied to (𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}) and the unique optimal solution of DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), which consists of 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} and its associated weights by Proposition 6.1. A positive match rate xi​j∗>0x^{*}_{ij}>0 makes the reward constraint for (i,j)(i,j) tight, so every acceptable match has a nonnegative score. Moreover, every nonempty set obtained by thresholding the positive scores carries a positive dual weight and therefore has a tight primal availability constraint. Each such set must be a prefix of ≻j\succ_{j}, which forces the policy to accept every positive-score match and rank acceptable partners by nonincreasing score. ∎

Proposition 6.2 completes the unifying picture promised at the beginning of this section. The primal approach constructs priorities by solving a linear program, without computing values, while the dual approach computes values as a fixed point, without solving a linear program. Nevertheless, when LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a suitable optimal solution, every policy that the primal approach constructs is also a value-based policy restricted to ℳ\mathcal{M}: whichever suitable optimal solution of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) the primal approach uses, the resulting policy accepts only matches in ℳ\mathcal{M} with nonnegative score ri​j−viℳ−vjℳr_{ij}-v^{\mathcal{M}}_{i}-v^{\mathcal{M}}_{j}, accepts every match in ℳ\mathcal{M} with a positive score, and ranks acceptable partners in decreasing order of score. In other words, the tight availability constraints that the primal approach reads from its solution agree with the ranking by score under the restricted fixed point. For the set returned by Algorithm 1, every pair in ℳ\mathcal{M} is used at a positive rate, so every pair in ℳ\mathcal{M} has a nonnegative score, and the policy of Section 4 accepts every match in ℳ\mathcal{M} with a positive score, possibly together with some matches of score zero.

6.3 Computing Values in Polynomial Time via LP

It remains to describe the computational requirements of the procedure: running Algorithm 1, solving DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), and sorting the acceptable partners of each arriving type by score. By Proposition 4.5, Algorithm 1 runs in polynomial time, since each program LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) can be solved in polynomial time (Proposition 4.4). Although DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has exponentially many variables, the ellipsoid method applied to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) also yields an exact optimal solution of DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) with only polynomially many nonzero weights (Grötschel et al. 1988). Formally, we have the following proposition.

Proposition 6.3.

For every ℳ⊆𝒯×𝒯\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}, an optimal solution of DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) with polynomially many nonzero weights zS​jz_{Sj} can be computed in time polynomial in the input size.

The proof is deferred to Section C.5.3. Combined with Proposition 4.5, this result gives the following computational consequence of the primal–dual connection.

Theorem 6.4.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the set of matches returned by Algorithm 1, and let (𝐯∗,𝐳∗)(\mathbf{v}^{*},\mathbf{z}^{*}) be an optimal solution of DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). Then 𝐯∗=𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{*}=\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} is the fixed point restricted to ℳ\mathcal{M}, every static priority policy consistent with the suitable optimal solution returned by Algorithm 1 is consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯∗\mathbf{v}^{*}, and every static priority policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯∗\mathbf{v}^{*} satisfies (22). Moreover, ℳ\mathcal{M}, 𝐯∗\mathbf{v}^{*}, and a static priority policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯∗\mathbf{v}^{*} can be computed in time polynomial in the input size.

Proof.

By Proposition 4.5, LPPOL​(ℳ)≥LPPOL​(𝒯×𝒯)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})\geq\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{T\times T}) and LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a suitable optimal solution, so Proposition 6.1 gives 𝐯∗=𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{*}=\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}, Proposition 6.2 gives the consistency claim, and Lemma 5.7 and the discussion following it in Section 5.4 give (22). Algorithm 1 solves at most |𝒯|2+1|\mathcal{T}|^{2}+1 linear programs of the form LPPOL​(⋅)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\cdot), since every iteration but the last removes a pair from the current set; each solve takes polynomial time by Proposition 4.4, the final solve of DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) takes polynomial time by Proposition 6.3, and sorting by score takes polynomial time as well. ∎

We close with two remarks. First, the values computed in this way solve the fixed-point equation restricted to the final set ℳ\mathcal{M}, but need not solve the unrestricted equation 𝐅⁡(𝐯)=𝐯\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{v} used in Theorem 5.5: a deleted pair may have a positive score under 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}. Second, the guarantee does not depend on which suitable optimal solution to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) is used to construct a policy consistent with it (Definition 4.1). By Proposition 6.2, every such policy is consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} and therefore satisfies (22). More generally, the same guarantee holds for every policy consistent with ℳ\mathcal{M} and 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}}, regardless of how ties among equal scores are broken.

7 Conclusion

Summary. We studied dynamic matching with abandonment, in which agents of different types arrive over time, wait in a common pool from which they may abandon, and are matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. We showed that a simple, deterministic static priority policy, computable in polynomial time, earns at least half of the omniscient benchmark, which is the best possible guarantee for online policies (Kessel et al. 2022). Two complementary approaches lead to this guarantee. The primal approach reads priority lists from the tight constraints of a family of linear programs and uses pruning to find a program with a suitable optimal solution. The dual approach computes one value per type, as the unique solution of a fixed-point equation, and ranks matches by their scores. Both approaches rest on the same lower bound on agent availability (Lemma 3.3), and they meet through the dual of these linear programs: the policies of the primal approach are value-based policies restricted to a set of allowed matches.

Future directions. Our analysis certifies the reward of a policy through linear programs, rather than by computing the stationary distribution of the underlying Markov chain. It is this approach that makes static priority policies tractable to analyze in markets with many types, type-specific arrival and abandonment rates, and general compatibility structures. We hope that these tools, and in particular the availability bound of Lemma 3.3, will prove useful in other stochastic matching and resource allocation problems in which simple policies are desirable.

Our work also suggests several directions for future research. First, in the general model of dynamic matching with abandonment, a natural goal is to improve upon the competitive ratio of one half against the optimal online policy, which is a weaker benchmark than the omniscient one. Second, one could study online learning and optimization versions of the model, in which parameters such as the arrival and abandonment rates or the rewards are unknown. Finally, it would be interesting to extend our results to more general arrival processes and sojourn-time distributions, or to settings in which rewards change over time, for example, as a function of how long an agent has waited.

Disclosure of AI Usage

One result in this paper was obtained with the help of an AI system. The proof that the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} can be computed in polynomial time for every set of matches ℳ\mathcal{M} (Proposition 5.4) was first found by OpenAI’s Codex Astra, after several rounds of prompting and interaction with the authors, and was subsequently verified and simplified by the authors. All other results are the authors’ own work. In particular, the authors established that, for the set ℳ\mathcal{M} returned by Algorithm 1, the restricted fixed point 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} is given by the unique optimal solution of the dual of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}), and can therefore be computed in polynomial time by linear programming (Propositions 6.1 and 6.3 and Theorem 6.4). Apart from the proof of Proposition 5.4, AI tools were used only to edit the writing.

Appendix A Further Related Work

This appendix complements Section 1 by positioning our model, results, and techniques within the broader literature on dynamic matching and online allocation in operations research, economics, and computer science.

Dynamic matching with abandonment. The guarantees known for our model and its special cases are summarized in Section 1.1 and Figure 1; here we describe the approaches behind them. Collina et al. (2020) and Aouad and Sarıtaç (2022) introduced the model independently. Collina et al. (2020) upper-bound the omniscient benchmark by a linear program and match according to its solution with a randomized policy. Aouad and Sarıtaç (2022) upper-bound the optimal online policy by a linear program and use a feasible solution of a quadratically constrained variant of this program to guide a randomized policy; they also study a cost-minimization version motivated by car-pooling. Li et al. (2026) design an LP-based randomized policy for a fully online model in which agents arrive i.i.d. over discrete time and have type-dependent sojourn-time distributions known only through their means; they extend its analysis to Poisson arrivals. When one side of the market must be matched upon arrival, Kessel et al. (2022) introduce the stationary prophet inequality and design pricing-based policies, and Patel and Wajc (2024) allow buyers with combinatorial demands and relate the guarantees achievable against their linear programming benchmark to offline contention resolution schemes. The relaxations in these papers have availability constraints for one waiting type at a time; AmaniHamedani et al. (2026) strengthen them to all subsets of waiting types and round the resulting program with correlated proposals. Our relaxation LPOMN\textup{LP}^{\textup{OMN}} extends these subset constraints to the general model (Section 2.3).

Other work approximates the optimal online policy arbitrarily well in structured settings. When one side must be matched upon arrival and all waiting agents abandon at a common rate, AmaniHamedani et al. (2025) use queue-length information to design adaptive policies that approximate the optimal online policy to within a factor of 1−ε1-\varepsilon, provided that the number of waiting types is constant or the instance is Euclidean of fixed dimension. They also show by example that, for this objective, adaptive policies can substantially outperform static ones on specific instances; by contrast, our results imply that static priority policies lose nothing relative to adaptive ones in terms of the worst-case ratio to the omniscient benchmark.

Prophet inequalities and Bayesian online allocation. Competitive analysis against the Bayesian omniscient benchmark follows the tradition of prophet inequalities. For a single item, a single threshold guarantees half of the expected maximum of independent nonnegative values, and no online policy can guarantee more (Krengel and Sucheston 1978, Samuel-Cahn 1984); our main result can be viewed as an analog of this fact for dynamic matching with abandonment, with static priority lists in place of the threshold. Prophet inequalities have since been extended to richer feasibility constraints, including matroids (Kleinberg and Weinberg 2019) and matchings (Gravin and Wang 2023, Ezra et al. 2022); for instance, Ezra et al. (2022) obtain the tight ratio of 12\tfrac{1}{2} for matchings in general graphs with vertex arrivals. Several of these guarantees can be obtained through prices that charge an allocation for the future value that it forecloses, a principle formalized by the balanced prices of Dütting et al. (2020); the values of our value-based policies play a similar role (Section 5). Another common approach solves an ex-ante relaxation and rounds its solution online, using tools such as the magician’s problem (Alaei 2014) and online contention resolution schemes (Feldman et al. 2021).

A related line of work compares policies with the optimal online policy instead of the prophet. For a single item, Niazadeh et al. (2018) show that the tight guarantees of single-threshold policies relative to the prophet remain tight relative to the optimal online policy; in contrast, in the single-good stationary prophet inequality, a posted-price policy earns at least 0.6560.656 of the reward of the optimal online policy (Kessel et al. 2022), more than the best possible ratio of 12\tfrac{1}{2} against the omniscient benchmark. Beyond single-item settings, Anari et al. (2019) give a polynomial-time approximation scheme relative to the optimal online policy for Bayesian online selection under laminar matroid constraints of constant depth and under production constraints, by strengthening the ex-ante relaxation into a hierarchy of linear programs. Papadimitriou et al. (2024) give a polynomial-time 0.510.51-approximation of the optimal online policy for online stochastic max-weight bipartite matching with vertex arrivals, together with PSPACE-hardness of approximating this policy within some constant.

Reusable resources. Online allocation of reusable resources, in which an allocated unit is occupied for some time and then returns to inventory, has been studied under stochastic (Rusmevichientong et al. 2020, Dickerson et al. 2021, Feng et al. 2024) and adversarial (Gong et al. 2022, Delong et al. 2024, Goyal et al. 2025) arrivals. With Poisson arrivals and kk units of each resource, Aminian et al. (2026a) attain a 1−2/(π​k)+O⁡(1/k)1-\sqrt{2/(\pi k)}+O(1/k) fraction of the omniscient benchmark, improving upon Feng et al. (2024), through a propose-then-admit scheme in which each resource runs a state-dependent admission-control policy; relatedly, Aminian et al. (2026b) introduce stationary online contention resolution schemes, in which the distribution of the selected set does not depend on the arrival order. Like ours, the analysis of Aminian et al. (2026a) relies on Poisson arrivals, steady-state arguments, and a linear program that bounds the omniscient benchmark. In reusable-resource models, however, a fixed set of resources cycles between busy and idle states, whereas in our model matched agents leave the system and future matching opportunities are created by new arrivals on every side of the market.

Online matching with arrivals and departures. In the classical online bipartite matching problem of Karp et al. (1990) and its variants with known arrival distributions (Feldman et al. 2009, Manshadi et al. 2012, Jaillet and Lu 2014), the vertices on one side are present throughout, and each vertex on the other side must be matched upon arrival or lost, so the policy never chooses when to match (see Mehta 2013 for a survey). In min-cost bipartite perfect matching with delays (Ashlagi et al. 2017), the algorithm does choose when to match, but waiting incurs a linear cost and no request abandons. In the adversarial fully online matching model, all vertices arrive online and remain available until a deadline, at which the algorithm can still match them; for unweighted matching, competitive ratios above 12\tfrac{1}{2} are achievable (Huang et al. 2019, Huang et al. 2020a, Huang et al. 2020b). For edge-weighted matching in general graphs with adversarial arrivals and structured departures, in which agents can be matched when they become critical, Ashlagi et al. (2023a) obtain constant competitive ratios and show that no algorithm is better than 12\tfrac{1}{2}-competitive. Truong and Wang (2019) study a finite-horizon two-sided model with stochastic arrivals, in which supply waits for a deterministic amount of time and demand must be matched upon arrival. In all of these models, the planner never loses an agent without warning: departures are known in advance, absent, or preceded by a last opportunity to match. In our model, the planner learns of an abandonment only after the agent has left.

Matching queues and large-market analysis. Dynamic matching also has a long history in applied probability, where work on matching rates under first-come-first-served policies (Caldentey et al. 2009, Adan and Weiss 2012) and on the stability of stochastic matching models (Bušić et al. 2013, Mairesse and Moyal 2016, Jonckheere et al. 2023) analyzes given policies rather than designing reward-maximizing ones. A control-oriented literature designs policies that are asymptotically optimal as the market grows (Gurvich and Ward 2014, Özkan and Ward 2020), in some cases only within natural classes of policies (Blanchet et al. 2022). Aveklouris et al. (2025) show that, with heterogeneous match values, holding costs, and general patience distributions on both sides, a state-independent priority policy that ranks the edges is asymptotically optimal when patience hazard rates are increasing; Liu et al. (2026) study a data-driven version of this problem. In a discrete-time model with abandonment, Hu and Zhou (2022) show that, under certain conditions on the rewards, the optimal policy matches type pairs according to a priority hierarchy, combined with thresholds. In contrast to this literature, our guarantee requires neither a large market nor structural assumptions on the rewards: it holds for every instance, including thin markets in which both the option value of waiting and the risk of abandonment matter.

Dynamic matching without abandonment. When agents never abandon, queues can grow, and policies can track the solution of a fluid relaxation. Under a general position condition, several policies attain constant regret relative to hindsight or fluid benchmarks (Kerimov et al. 2024, Gupta 2024, Wei et al. 2026). Under the same condition, Kerimov et al. (2025) show that, in two-way matching networks, a greedy static priority policy is hindsight optimal when the residual network of matches is acyclic (e.g., in two-sided networks), and Kerimov et al. (2026) show that policies that only observe which queues are nonempty, including a static priority policy for acyclic networks, can attain the optimal regret. With abandonment, the gap to the omniscient benchmark can instead grow linearly over time: even in the single-good stationary prophet inequality, no online policy can guarantee more than half of the omniscient benchmark (Kessel et al. 2022).

Market thickness, departure information, and other objectives. A complementary literature studies when to match in markets with random compatibility, typically measuring the fraction of agents who leave unmatched or their waiting times rather than the total weighted reward. Akbarpour et al. (2020) show that, when the planner knows which agents are about to leave, waiting to thicken the market can sharply reduce the fraction of agents who leave unmatched, whereas without this information, greedy matching is nearly optimal; Ashlagi et al. (2023b) show that greedy matching is also asymptotically optimal in large imbalanced markets. Baccara et al. (2020) characterize optimal dynamic matching with waiting costs and match values that depend on the types of both agents. Closer to the queueing formulation, Kohlenberg and Gurvich (2025) derive nonasymptotic scaling laws for the loss caused by abandonment in two-sided matching queues, and Kohlenberg (2025) identifies conditions under which restricting the compatibility graph and then matching greedily is scale-optimal, a policy structure close in spirit to static priority policies. In contrast to these papers, our guarantee allows arbitrary type-dependent rewards, is multiplicative, and holds for every instance.

Applications. The applications that motivate our model have extensive literatures of their own, including work on kidney exchange (Roth et al. 2004, Roth et al. 2005, Ünver 2010, Anderson et al. 2017, Ashlagi et al. 2018, Agarwal et al. 2019, Ashlagi and Roth 2021), deceased-donor organ allocation (Bertsimas et al. 2013, Agarwal et al. 2021), public and affordable housing (Arnosti and Shi 2020, Waldinger 2021, Leshno 2022), and homeless services (Azizi et al. 2018, Arnosti and Simon 2026). These papers address application-specific questions, such as incentives, fairness, equilibrium behavior, and empirical performance, which complement our worst-case analysis of a common stochastic matching primitive.

Appendix B Poisson Processes: Definitions and Proofs

This appendix complements Section 2.2: it gives the formal definition of a Poisson process and the marking property, proves Lemma 2.1, derives the consequence of Fact 2.1 that our analysis uses, and proves Corollary 2.2. For further background on Poisson processes, see Last and Penrose (2017).

A Poisson process with rate λ⁡(s)\lambda(s) is a way to formalize the idea of creating a random set Φ\Phi in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} by taking each tiny volume d​sds in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and including it in Φ\Phi with probability λ⁡(s)​d​s\lambda(s)ds independently.

Definition B.1 (Poisson process).

A Poisson process Φ\Phi on a Borel set 𝒳\mathcal{X} ⊆ℝn\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} with locally integrable rate function λ:𝒳→[0,∞)\lambda:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty) is a random set of countably many points in 𝒳\mathcal{X} such that:

  1. 1.

    For any Borel-measurable set I⊆𝒳I\mathrel{\subseteq}\mathcal{X}, |Φ∩I||\Phi\cap I| is a Poisson random variable with mean ∫Iλ⁡(s)​𝑑s\int_{I}\lambda(s)ds.

  2. 2.

    For any finite collection of disjoint Borel-measurable sets I1,I2,…,IkI_{1},I_{2},\ldots,I_{k} each contained in 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the random variables |Φ∩Ij||\Phi\cap I_{j}| are independent of each other.

We allow general rate functions on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} because marking (Fact B.1) produces Poisson processes on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with nonconstant rates, such as the process of arrival times and sojourn times of the agents of a given type.

The theory of Poisson processes shows that such a Φ\Phi exists. When we say that the agents arrive according to a Poisson process at rate λ⁡(s)=λ\lambda(s)=\lambda, we are formalizing the idea that an average of λ\lambda agents arrive in every unit of time, but the arrival of agents is independent across time.

The following property concerns points that carry independent random marks, such as the sojourn times of arriving agents (see, e.g., Last and Penrose 2017, Section 5.2).

Fact B.1 (Marking).

If Φ\Phi is a Poisson process on a Borel set 𝒳⊆ℝn\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} with rate function λ⁡(s)\lambda(s), and, given Φ\Phi, the points s∈Φs\in\Phi are associated with i.i.d. random variables Ys∈ℝY_{s}\in\mathbb{R} with density ff, then {(s,Ys):s∈Φ}\{(s,Y_{s}):s\in\Phi\} is a Poisson process on 𝒳×ℝ\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R} with rate function λ⁡(s)​f​(y)\lambda(s)f(y).

In the setting of our paper, agents of type ii, arriving according to a Poisson process, are associated with independent sojourn times that are exponentially distributed with mean 1μi\frac{1}{\mu_{i}}. Thus, by Fact B.1, the pairs of arrival times and sojourn times of type-ii agents form a Poisson process as well.

It is useful for us to understand the number of agents of any particular type present at any time. This number is described by Lemma 2.1 in Section 2.2, which is a simple consequence of Fact B.1. We restate it here and give its proof.

See 2.1

Proof.

By Fact B.1, the type-ii pairs (s,ℓ)(s,\ell) of arrival times ss and sojourn times ℓ\ell (so that the departure time is s+ℓs+\ell) form a Poisson process on [0,∞)×[0,∞)[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty) with rate (s,ℓ)↦λi​μi​e−μi​ℓ(s,\ell)\mapsto\lambda_{i}\mu_{i}e^{-\mu_{i}\ell}.

The agents that are present at time tt are exactly the points in:

R={(s,ℓ):0≤s≤t,ℓ>t−s}.R=\{(s,\ell):0\leq s\mathrel{\leq}t,\ \ell>t-s\}.

By Definition B.1, the number of such points is Poisson with mean

∫Rλi​μi​e−μi​ℓ​𝑑ℓ​𝑑s=λi​∫0t∫t−s∞μi​e−μi​ℓ​𝑑ℓ​𝑑s=λi​∫0te−μi​(t−s)​𝑑s=λiμi​(1−e−μi​t).\int_{R}\lambda_{i}\mu_{i}e^{-\mu_{i}\ell}\,d\ell\,ds=\lambda_{i}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{t-s}^{\infty}\mu_{i}e^{-\mu_{i}\ell}\,d\ell\,ds=\lambda_{i}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\mu_{i}(t-s)}\,ds=\tfrac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}\big(1-e^{-\mu_{i}t}\big).

The counts are independent across types because the arrival and sojourn processes are independent across types. ∎

The formula in Fact 2.1 is an expression of the fact that, conditional on a Poisson process having a point at a given location, the remaining points still form a Poisson process with the same rate function (Slivnyak 1962, Mecke 1967). See Coeurjolly et al. (2017) for a modern exposition, where this formula appears as equation (17)(17). A particularly useful corollary that we will apply is the following:

Corollary B.1.

Fix a type jj of agents with arrival rate λj\lambda_{j}. If, for each s≥0s\geq 0, E⁡(s)E(s) is an event determined by the history ℋ⁡(s)\mathcal{H}(s) of the agents that arrived before time ss, then for every t≥0t\geq 0,

𝔼⁡[∑a∈𝒜j​(t)(E⁡(ta))]=λj​∫0tℙ⁡(E⁡(s))​𝑑s.\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{j}(t)}\mathbf{1}\!\left(E(t_{a})\right)\right]=\lambda_{j}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{P}\left(E(s)\right)ds.
Proof.

Let Φ\Phi be the Poisson process of pairs of arrival times and sojourn times of type-jj agents, which has rate function (s,ℓ)↦λj​μj​e−μj​ℓ(s,\ell)\mapsto\lambda_{j}\mu_{j}e^{-\mu_{j}\ell} by Fact B.1, and let Ψ\Psi collect the arrival times and sojourn times of the agents of all other types. Since Ψ\Psi is independent of Φ\Phi, we may condition on Ψ\Psi and apply Fact 2.1 to Φ\Phi with

g⁡((s,ℓ),φ)=(s<t)​(E⁡(s)​ occurs when the type-j agents are given by ​φ​ and the others by ​Ψ).g\big((s,\ell),\varphi\big)=\mathbf{1}\!\left(s<t\right)\,\mathbf{1}\!\left(E(s)\text{ occurs when the type-$j$ agents are given by }\varphi\text{ and the others by }\Psi\right).

For a type-jj agent aa, whose arrival and sojourn times form the point x∈Φx\in\Phi, the event E⁡(ta)E(t_{a}) depends only on the agents that arrived before tat_{a}, which do not include aa itself, so g⁡(x,Φ∖{x})=(ta<t)​(E⁡(ta))g(x,\Phi\setminus\{x\})=\mathbf{1}\!\left(t_{a}<t\right)\mathbf{1}\!\left(E(t_{a})\right). Similarly, g⁡((s,ℓ),Φ)=(s<t)​(E⁡(s))g\big((s,\ell),\Phi\big)=\mathbf{1}\!\left(s<t\right)\mathbf{1}\!\left(E(s)\right) by definition. Fact 2.1 therefore gives

𝔼⁡[∑a∈𝒜j​(t)(E⁡(ta))|Ψ]=∫0t∫0∞ℙ⁡(E⁡(s)∣Ψ)​λj​μj​e−μj​ℓ​𝑑ℓ​𝑑s=λj​∫0tℙ⁡(E⁡(s)∣Ψ)​𝑑s,\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{j}(t)}\mathbf{1}\!\left(E(t_{a})\right)\ \Big|\ \Psi\right]=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(E(s)\mid\Psi\right)\,\lambda_{j}\mu_{j}e^{-\mu_{j}\ell}\,d\ell\,ds=\lambda_{j}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{P}\left(E(s)\mid\Psi\right)\,ds,

and taking expectations over Ψ\Psi completes the proof. ∎

See 2.2

Proof.

Suppose first that π\pi is deterministic. Since π\pi is online, the state 𝐍π​(s)\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(s) just before time ss is determined by the arrivals and departures that occur before time ss. Hence, for each ss, the event {𝐍π(s)∈C}\{\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(s)\in C\} depends only on the history before time ss, and the first claim follows from Corollary B.1. If π\pi uses randomization that is independent of the arrival and sojourn processes, the same argument applies conditionally on this randomization. For the second claim, divide the first by tt and note that 1t​∫0tℙ⁡(𝐍π​(s)∈C)​𝑑s→p\tfrac{1}{t}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(s)\in C\right)\,ds\to p whenever ℙ⁡(𝐍π​(s)∈C)→p\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(s)\in C\right)\to p. ∎

C.2 Omitted Proofs from Section 3

See 3.1 Fix a static priority policy π\pi. The state only changes when an agent arrives or abandons the system, so from a state 𝐧\mathbf{n}, the time to the next transition follows an exponential distribution with rate ∑i∈𝒯(λi+ni​μi)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}(\lambda_{i}+n_{i}\mu_{i}), and the next state depends only on 𝐧\mathbf{n}. Therefore, 𝐍π​(t)\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t) is a continuous-time Markov chain. Note that the state changes only finitely many times (almost surely) in any finite interval.

Let 𝒩π\mathcal{N}^{\pi} be the set of states reachable from the empty state under policy π\pi. (Note that 𝒩π\mathcal{N}^{\pi} does indeed depend on π\pi: for example, if π\pi makes all matches as soon as possible, then 𝒩π\mathcal{N}^{\pi} is the set of states with at most one agent available.) The chain is irreducible on 𝒩π\mathcal{N}^{\pi}, since from any state, the empty state is reached with positive probability within any interval of positive length (if all available agents abandon before the next arrival), and every state of 𝒩π\mathcal{N}^{\pi} is reachable from the empty state by definition.

It remains to prove ergodicity, for which we apply the Foster–Lyapunov drift criterion of Prieto-Rumeau and Hernández-Lerma (2016, Theorem 2.8): it suffices to exhibit a nonnegative function WW on the state space, a finite set CC, and constants c>0c>0 and b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} such that

where q𝐧𝐧′q_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^{\prime}} is the transition rate from 𝐧\mathbf{n} to 𝐧′\mathbf{n}^{\prime}. Take W⁡(𝐧)=∑i∈𝒯niW(\mathbf{n})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}n_{i}, the total number of available agents. Thus (25) holds, and the chain is ergodic and has a unique stationary distribution.
