We conclude that:

𝔼⁡[Niπ]=limt→∞𝔼⁡[Niπ​(t)].\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}^{\pi}\right]=\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}^{\pi}(t)\right].

Finally, let Ci​jπC_{ij}^{\pi} be the set of states in which an arriving type-jj agent is matched to an available type-ii agent. Since every (i,j)(i,j) match is made when a type-jj agent arrives, based on the state just before its arrival, we have Xi​jπ​(t)=∑a∈𝒜j​(t)(𝐍π​(ta)∈Ci​jπ)X_{ij}^{\pi}(t)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{j}(t)}\mathbf{1}\!\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(t_{a})\in C_{ij}^{\pi}\right). Moreover, ℙ⁡(𝐍π​(s)∈Ci​jπ)→ℙ⁡(𝐍π∈Ci​jπ)\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(s)\in C_{ij}^{\pi}\right)\to\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}\in C_{ij}^{\pi}\right) as s→∞s\to\infty, because the state space is countable and 𝐍π​(s)\mathbf{N}^{\pi}(s) converges in distribution. Since π\pi is online, applying Corollary 2.2 with C=Ci​jπC=C_{ij}^{\pi} gives

xi​jπ=limt→∞1t​𝔼​[Xi​jπ​(t)]=λj​ℙ​(𝐍π∈Ci​jπ).x_{ij}^{\pi}=\lim_{t\to\infty}\tfrac{1}{t}\mathbb{E}\left[X_{ij}^{\pi}(t)\right]=\lambda_{j}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}\in C_{ij}^{\pi}\right).

Consequently, the limit V⁡(π)=limt→∞V⁡(π,t)V(\pi)=\lim_{t\to\infty}V(\pi,t) also exists. Indeed, V⁡(π,t)=∑i,j∈𝒯ri​j​xi​jπ​(t){V(\pi,t)=\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{T}}r_{ij}\,x_{ij}^{\pi}(t)} is a finite linear combination of the rates xi​jπ​(t)x_{ij}^{\pi}(t), each of which converges to xi​jπx_{ij}^{\pi}, so V⁡(π)=∑i,j∈𝒯ri​j​xi​jπ{V(\pi)=\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{T}}r_{ij}\,x_{ij}^{\pi}}.

See 3.2

Proof.

Recall that Niπ​(t)N_{i}^{\pi}(t) represents the number of type-ii agents available just before time tt and Xi​jπ​(t)X_{ij}^{\pi}(t) is the number of (i,j)(i,j) matches made before time tt. The proof of Equation (4) was already shown using the linearity argument at the end of the proof of Lemma 3.1, so it remains to prove (SP-Balance) and (SP-Availability).

Constraint (SP-Balance).

Let Diπ​(t)D_{i}^{\pi}(t) denote the number of type-ii agents that have abandoned the system (departed unmatched) by time tt. Then for any time tt and any i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T}, we have:

Diπ​(t)+Niπ​(t)+∑j∈𝒯Xi​jπ​(t)+∑j∈𝒯Xj​iπ​(t)=|𝒜i​(t)|.D_{i}^{\pi}(t)+N_{i}^{\pi}(t)+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}X^{\pi}_{ij}(t)+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}X_{ji}^{\pi}(t)=|\mathcal{A}_{i}(t)|. (26)

This says that each agent who arrives before time tt has either abandoned, been matched with another agent, or is still available. Note that:

𝔼⁡[Diπ​(t)]=𝔼⁡[μi​∫0tNiπ​(s)​𝑑s],\mathbb{E}\left[D_{i}^{\pi}(t)\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\mu_{i}\int_{0}^{t}N_{i}^{\pi}(s)ds\right],

because for any static priority policy π\pi, Diπ​(t)−μi​∫0tNiπ​(s)​𝑑sD_{i}^{\pi}(t)-\mu_{i}\int_{0}^{t}N_{i}^{\pi}(s)ds is a martingale (Pang et al. 2007, see, e.g.,). So by taking expectations, dividing by tt, and taking the limit as t→∞t\to\infty in (26), constraint (SP-Balance) follows.

Constraint (SP-Availability).

Let Ci​jπC_{ij}^{\pi} be the set of states in which an arriving type-jj agent is matched to an available type-ii agent. Note that we showed (using Corollary 2.2) in the proof of Lemma 3.1 that:

xi​jπ=λj​ℙ​(𝐍π∈Ci​jπ).x_{ij}^{\pi}=\lambda_{j}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}\in C_{ij}^{\pi}\right).

The events {Ci​jπ:i∈𝒯}\{C_{ij}^{\pi}:i\in\mathcal{T}\} are disjoint, so

∑i∈Sxi​jπ=λj​ℙ​(𝐍π∈⋃i∈SCi​jπ).\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij}^{\pi}=\lambda_{j}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbf{N}^{\pi}\in\bigcup_{i\in S}C_{ij}^{\pi}\right).

The event on the right can occur only if some type in SS is available, so (SP-Availability) follows. Furthermore, if S∈Prefixes(≻j)S\in\text{Prefixes}(\succ_{j}), then SS consists of the highest-ranked acceptable types for jj, so whenever some type in SS is available the best acceptable available type already lies in SS and the arriving type-jj agent is matched into SS. Thus

{∑i∈SNiπ>0}={𝐍π∈⋃i∈SCi​jπ},\left\{\textstyle\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi}>0\right\}=\left\{\mathbf{N}^{\pi}\in\bigcup_{i\in S}C_{ij}^{\pi}\right\},

so (SP-Availability) holds with equality. ∎

Before proving Lemma 3.3, we define the IIA property that all static priority policies satisfy, and prove a crucial lemma that holds for any IIA policy.

Fix a policy π\pi. Throughout our discussion, we will omit π\pi from the notation. Recall that for t≥0t\geq 0, we write 𝐍⁡(t)=(Ni​(t))i∈𝒯\mathbf{N}(t)=(N_{i}(t))_{i\in\mathcal{T}} for the state at time tt after running policy π\pi, with Ni​(t)N_{i}(t) representing the number of type-ii agents available just before time tt. Furthermore, 𝒜i​(t)\mathcal{A}_{i}(t) is the set of agents of type ii that arrive before time tt, and

ℋ⁡(t)={(ia,ta,da)}a∈𝒜⁡(t)\mathcal{H}(t)=\{(i_{a},t_{a},d_{a})\}_{a\in\mathcal{A}(t)}

is the history up to time tt. Let 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} denote the ii-th unit vector.

Let us abuse the notation slightly and define 𝐍⁡(t,ℋ)\mathbf{N}(t;\mathcal{H}) to be the state at time tt obtained by applying the deterministic policy π\pi to a deterministic history ℋ\mathcal{H}. For an additional agent aa of type ii, write ℋ∪{a}\mathcal{H}\cup\{a\} for the history with aa added, and let Qa​(t,ℋ)Q_{a}(t;\mathcal{H}) be the indicator that this added agent is available at time tt when the policy is run on ℋ∪{a}\mathcal{H}\cup\{a\}.

Definition C.1 (IIA property).

A policy satisfies independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA) if, for every deterministic history ℋ\mathcal{H}, every t≥0t\geq 0, and every added agent aa:

Qa​(t,ℋ)=1⟹𝐍⁡(t,ℋ∪{a})=𝐍⁡(t,ℋ)+eia.Q_{a}(t;\mathcal{H})=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathbf{N}(t;\mathcal{H}\cup\{a\})=\mathbf{N}(t;\mathcal{H})+e_{i_{a}}. (IIA)

In other words, if the added agent aa is still available at time tt, the rest of the system is at exactly the state it would have reached had agent aa never arrived.

Suppose we fix a deterministic rule for choosing among agents of the same type, under which removing an unselected agent does not change the selection; for example, always choose the earliest-arriving agent of the selected type. By Footnote 8 this is without loss of generality for Lemma 3.3, since the distribution of 𝐍π\mathbf{N}^{\pi} does not depend on the tie-breaking rule. Once we fix such a rule, we claim that any static priority policy satisfies Definition C.1.

To see this, compare two systems: one run on ℋ\mathcal{H}, and the other run on ℋ∪{a}\mathcal{H}\cup\{a\}, with both using the same arrival and sojourn times for all agents in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Up to time tat_{a}, the two systems coincide. Since Qa​(t,ℋ)=1Q_{a}(t;\mathcal{H})=1, agent aa does not get matched upon its arrival, so the systems continue to coincide immediately after time tat_{a}, except for the addition of agent aa.

Between time tat_{a} and tt, the abandonments coincide in both systems. Consider an arrival after time tat_{a}. Since Qa​(t,ℋ)=1Q_{a}(t;\mathcal{H})=1, this arrival is not matched to aa in the system with ℋ∪{a}\mathcal{H}\cup\{a\}. Otherwise, the static priority policy selects the same agent to match in both systems. Thus all original agents have the same status at time tt in the two systems, and the only difference is the additional available type-ii agent aa. This is exactly what is needed in Definition C.1.

Thus, every static priority policy satisfies the IIA property. The following lemma about policies satisfying the IIA property is the main stochastic step in the proof of Lemma 3.3.

Lemma C.1.

Suppose that a policy π\pi satisfies IIA. Then, for every i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T}, every t≥0t\geq 0, and every bounded nonnegative measurable function h:ℕ𝒯→ℝ≥0h:\mathbb{N}^{\mathcal{T}}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0},

𝔼⁡[Ni​(t)​h​(𝐍⁡(t)−𝐞i)]≤λiμi​(1−e−μi​t)​𝔼​[h⁡(𝐍⁡(t))],\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}(t)h(\mathbf{N}(t)-\mathbf{e}_{i})\right]\leq\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}\left(1-e^{-\mu_{i}t}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[h(\mathbf{N}(t))\right], (27)

where the term Ni​(t)​h​(𝐍⁡(t)−𝐞i)N_{i}(t)h(\mathbf{N}(t)-\mathbf{e}_{i}) is defined to be zero if Ni​(t)=0N_{i}(t)=0. Hence, if for the policy π\pi its induced 𝐍⁡(t)\mathbf{N}(t) converges in distribution to 𝐍\mathbf{N}, where 𝐍\mathbf{N} is drawn from the stationary distribution (for example, if π\pi is a static priority policy, Lemma 3.1),

𝔼⁡[Ni​h​(𝐍−𝐞i)]≤λiμi​𝔼​[h⁡(𝐍)].\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}h(\mathbf{N}-\mathbf{e}_{i})\right]\leq\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}\mathbb{E}\left[h(\mathbf{N})\right].
Proof.

To start, notice that Ni​(t)​h​(𝐍⁡(t)−𝐞i)N_{i}(t)h(\mathbf{N}(t)-\mathbf{e}_{i}) is just a sum of h⁡(𝐍⁡(t)−𝐞i)h(\mathbf{N}(t)-\mathbf{e}_{i}) over the available type-ii agents, and furthermore, that every available type-ii agent aa at time tt satisfies:

𝐍⁡(t)−𝐞i=𝐍⁡(t,ℋ⁡(t)∖{a})\mathbf{N}(t)-\mathbf{e}_{i}=\mathbf{N}(t;\mathcal{H}(t)\setminus\{a\})

by (IIA) (applied with ℋ=ℋ⁡(t)∖{a}\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}(t)\setminus\{a\}). Therefore:

Ni​(t)​h​(𝐍⁡(t)−𝐞i)=∑a∈𝒜i​(t)Qa​(t,ℋ⁡(t)∖{a})​h​(𝐍⁡(t,ℋ⁡(t)∖{a})),\displaystyle N_{i}(t)h(\mathbf{N}(t)-\mathbf{e}_{i})=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{i}(t)}Q_{a}(t;\mathcal{H}(t)\setminus\{a\})h\left(\mathbf{N}(t;\mathcal{H}(t)\setminus\{a\})\right),

Next, we take the expectation on both sides, using the Slivnyak–Mecke formula (Fact 2.1). Let Φ\Phi be the Poisson process on [0,∞)2[0,\infty)^{2} of type-ii arrival and sojourn time pairs (Fact B.1), and let Ψ\Psi collect the arrival and sojourn times of the agents of all other types, which are independent of Φ\Phi. Conditional on Ψ\Psi, we apply Fact 2.1 to Φ\Phi with g⁡(a,φ)=Qa​(t,φ∪Ψ)​h​(𝐍⁡(t,φ∪Ψ))g(a,\varphi)=Q_{a}(t;\varphi\cup\Psi)\,h(\mathbf{N}(t;\varphi\cup\Psi)), where φ∪Ψ\varphi\cup\Psi denotes the history formed by the type-ii agents in φ\varphi and the other agents in Ψ\Psi, and then average over Ψ\Psi, as in the proof of Corollary B.1. This gives:

𝔼⁡[Ni​(t)​h​(𝐍⁡(t)−𝐞i)]=λi​∫0t∫0∞𝔼⁡[Qa​(t,ℋ⁡(t))​h​(𝐍⁡(t,ℋ⁡(t)))]​μi​e−μi​ℓ​𝑑ℓ​𝑑s,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}(t)h(\mathbf{N}(t)-\mathbf{e}_{i})\right]=\lambda_{i}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[Q_{a}(t;\mathcal{H}(t))h(\mathbf{N}(t;\mathcal{H}(t)))\right]\mu_{i}e^{-\mu_{i}\ell}d\ell ds,

where, in the integrand, aa denotes a type-ii agent with ta=st_{a}=s, sa=ℓs_{a}=\ell, and da=s+ℓd_{a}=s+\ell. λi​μi​e−μi​ℓ​d​ℓ​d​s\lambda_{i}\mu_{i}e^{-\mu_{i}\ell}d\ell ds is the rate of the Poisson process associated with type-ii arrival and sojourn time pairs. Now clearly, an agent can be available at tt only if it has not yet abandoned, so

Qa​(t,ℋ⁡(t))≤(da>t)=(s+ℓ>t).Q_{a}(t;\mathcal{H}(t))\leq\mathbf{1}\!\left(d_{a}>t\right)=\mathbf{1}\!\left(s+\ell>t\right).

It follows that,

𝔼⁡[Ni​(t)​h​(𝐍⁡(t)−𝐞i)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}(t)h(\mathbf{N}(t)-\mathbf{e}_{i})\right] ≤𝔼⁡[h⁡(𝐍⁡(t))]​λi​μi​∫0t∫0∞(s+ℓ>t)​e−μi​ℓ​𝑑ℓ​𝑑s\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[h(\mathbf{N}(t))\right]\lambda_{i}\mu_{i}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathbf{1}\!\left(s+\ell>t\right)\,e^{-\mu_{i}\ell}\,d\ell\,ds
=𝔼⁡[h⁡(𝐍⁡(t))]​λi​∫0te−μi​(t−s)​𝑑s\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[h(\mathbf{N}(t))\right]\lambda_{i}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\mu_{i}(t-s)}ds
=λiμi​(1−e−μi​t)​𝔼​[h⁡(𝐍⁡(t))],\displaystyle=\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}\left(1-e^{-\mu_{i}t}\right)\mathbb{E}\left[h(\mathbf{N}(t))\right],

as desired. As t→∞t\to\infty, 𝐍⁡(t)\mathbf{N}(t) converges in distribution to 𝐍\mathbf{N}, while Ni​(t)N_{i}(t) is uniformly integrable, since it is dominated by the number of type-ii agents present at time tt, a Poisson variable with mean λiμi​(1−e−μi​t)≤λiμi\tfrac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}\left(1-e^{-\mu_{i}t}\right)\leq\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}. So both sides of (27) converge and the inequality passes to the stationary distribution:

𝔼⁡[Ni​h​(𝐍−𝐞i)]≤λiμi​𝔼​[h⁡(𝐍)],\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}h(\mathbf{N}-\mathbf{e}_{i})\right]\leq\tfrac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}\mathbb{E}\left[h(\mathbf{N})\right],

as needed. ∎

We are now ready to complete the proof of Lemma 3.3.

See 3.3

Proof.

Fix a nonempty S⊆𝒯S\subseteq\mathcal{T} (for S=∅S=\emptyset, both sides of (6) are zero) and define NS≜∑i∈SNiN_{S}\triangleq\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}. Let pm=ℙ⁡(NS=m),p_{m}=\mathbb{P}\left(N_{S}=m\right), and apply Lemma C.1 with

h⁡(𝐍)=(∑k∈SNk=m).h(\mathbf{N})=\mathbf{1}\!\left(\textstyle\sum_{k\in S}N_{k}=m\right).

For each i∈Si\in S, we conclude that:

𝔼⁡[Ni​(NS=m+1)]≤λiμi​pm,\mathbb{E}\left[N_{i}\mathbf{1}\!\left(N_{S}=m+1\right)\right]\leq\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\mu_{i}}p_{m},

so summing over i∈Si\in S gives

(m+1)​pm+1≤ρ⁡(S)​pm.(m+1)p_{m+1}\leq\rho(S)p_{m}. (28)

Let LSL_{S} be a Poisson random variable with mean ρ⁡(S)\rho(S), and let lm=ℙ⁡(LS=m)l_{m}=\mathbb{P}\left(L_{S}=m\right). Since LSL_{S} satisfies (28) with equality, i.e., (m+1)​lm+1=ρ⁡(S)​lm(m+1)l_{m+1}=\rho(S)l_{m}, the likelihood ratios qm=pmlmq_{m}=\frac{p_{m}}{l_{m}} are nonincreasing in mm. So NSN_{S}, conditioned on being positive, is stochastically dominated by LSL_{S}, i.e., for any k≥1k\geq 1,

ℙ⁡(NS≥k∣NS>0)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(N_{S}\geq k\mid N_{S}>0\right) =∑m≥kqm​lm∑m≥1qm​lm≤∑m≥klm∑m≥1lm=ℙ⁡(LS≥k∣LS>0),\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{m\geq k}q_{m}l_{m}}{\sum_{m\geq 1}q_{m}l_{m}}\leq\frac{\sum_{m\geq k}l_{m}}{\sum_{m\geq 1}l_{m}}=\mathbb{P}\left(L_{S}\geq k\mid L_{S}>0\right), (29)

where the inequality follows because rm′≤rmr_{m^{\prime}}\leq r_{m} for m′≥k>mm^{\prime}\geq k>m. Summing (29) over k≥1k\geq 1 turns this tail comparison into a comparison of conditional means:

𝔼⁡[NS]ℙ⁡(NS>0)=𝔼⁡[NS∣NS>0]≤𝔼⁡[LS∣LS>0]=ρ⁡(S)1−e−ρ⁡(S)=1γS.\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[N_{S}\right]}{\mathbb{P}\left(N_{S}>0\right)}=\mathbb{E}\left[N_{S}\mid N_{S}>0\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[L_{S}\mid L_{S}>0\right]=\frac{\rho(S)}{1-e^{-\rho(S)}}\mathrel{=}\frac{1}{\gamma_{S}}.

Since 𝔼⁡[NS]=∑i∈Sniπ\mathbb{E}\left[N_{S}\right]=\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}^{\pi}, rearranging gives (6). This proves the desired result. ∎

C.3.1 Proofs from Section 4.2

Proof.

Write (𝐧,𝐱)=(𝐧∗,𝐱∗)({\bf n},{\bf x})=({\bf n}^{*},{\bf x}^{*}) for the optimal solution in the statement. Let (𝐧π,𝐱π)({{\bf n}}^{\pi},{{\bf x}}^{\pi}) be the steady-state quantities of π\pi defined in (3). We show that (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) can be expressed as a convex combination of (𝐧π,𝐱π)({{\bf n}}^{\pi},{{\bf x}}^{\pi}) and a feasible point (𝐧^,𝐱^)(\hat{\bf n},\hat{\bf x}) of LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}). β​𝐱π+(1−β)​𝐱^=𝐱.\beta{{\bf x}}^{\pi}+(1-\beta)\hat{{{\bf x}}}={{\bf x}}. (30)

Since π\pi makes matches only in ℳ\mathcal{M}, (4) gives V⁡(π)=∑(i,j)∈ℳri​j​xi​jπ=𝐫∘𝐱πV(\pi)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}}r_{ij}x^{\pi}_{ij}=\mathbf{r}\circ{\bf x}^{\pi}, and therefore V⁡(π)≥𝐫∘𝐱=LPPOL​(ℳ)V(\pi)\geq\mathbf{r}\circ{\bf x}=\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}).

Given β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) define

x^i​j\displaystyle\hat{x}_{ij} =xi​j−β​xi​jπ1−β\displaystyle=\frac{x_{ij}-\beta x_{ij}^{\pi}}{1-\beta} ∀(i,j)∈ℳ,\displaystyle\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}, (31)
n^i\displaystyle\hat{n}_{i} =ni−β​niπ1−β\displaystyle=\frac{n_{i}-\beta n_{i}^{\pi}}{1-\beta} ∀i∈𝒯.\displaystyle\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{T}. (32)

Then (30) holds by construction. We will show that (𝐧^,𝐱^)(\hat{{{\bf n}}},\hat{{{\bf x}}}) is feasible for all sufficiently small β\beta.

We first show that 𝐱^\hat{{\bf x}} is nonnegative. If xi​j=0x_{ij}=0, then by the definition of consistency, ii is not acceptable to jj according to π\pi. Therefore xi​jπ=0x_{ij}^{\pi}=0 and x^i​j=0\hat{x}_{ij}=0. Meanwhile, if xi​j>0x_{ij}>0, then x^i​j>0\hat{x}_{ij}>0 for all sufficiently small β\beta. Similarly, 𝐧^≥0\hat{{\bf n}}\geq 0 for all sufficiently small β\beta, because ni>0n_{i}>0 for every i∈𝒯i\in\mathcal{T}, as we show in the proof of Lemma 4.3 in Section C.3.2, which does not use Proposition 4.2.

Turning to (P-Balance), this holds for both (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) (because (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) is feasible for LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M})) and for (𝐧π,𝐱π)({\bf n}^{\pi},{\bf x}^{\pi}) (by Lemma 3.2, since xi​jπ=0x^{\pi}_{ij}=0 for (i,j)∉ℳ(i,j)\notin\mathcal{M}). Because (P-Balance) is a linear equality constraint, it also holds for any affine combination of (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) and (𝐧π,𝐱π)({\bf n}^{\pi},{\bf x}^{\pi}), that is, any combination whose coefficients sum to one, and in particular for (𝐧^,𝐱^)(\hat{{{\bf n}}},\hat{{{\bf x}}}).

It remains to show that (P-Availability) holds. We wish to show that for all j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T} and all nonempty S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}, the following quantity is nonnegative:

(1−β)​(λj​γS​∑i∈Sn^i−∑i∈Sx^i​j)=(λj​γS​∑i∈Sni−∑i∈Sxi​j)−β⁡(λj​γS​∑i∈Sniπ−∑i∈Sxi​jπ).(1-\beta)(\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}\hat{n}_{i}-\sum_{i\in S}\hat{x}_{ij})=(\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}-\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij})-\beta(\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}^{\pi}-\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij}^{\pi}). (Note that this equality follows immediately from (31) and (32).) If (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) satisfies (P-Availability) strictly, then the first term on the right side of (33) is positive and thus the entire expression is positive for sufficiently small β\beta. If (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}) satisfies (P-Availability) with equality, then the first term on the right side of (33) is zero and S∈𝒫j​(𝐧,𝐱)S\in\mathcal{P}_{j}({\bf n},{\bf x}). Because π\pi is consistent with (𝐧,𝐱)({\bf n},{\bf x}), SS must be a prefix of ≻j\succ_{j}. Applying Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3, we conclude that

∑i∈Sxi​jπ=λj​ℙ​(∑i∈SNiπ>0)≥λj​γS​∑i∈Sniπ,\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij}^{\pi}=\lambda_{j}\mathbb{P}\left(\sum_{i\in S}N_{i}^{\pi}>0\right)\geq\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}n_{i}^{\pi},

and therefore the expression in (33) is nonnegative. Since LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has finitely many constraints, all of them hold for every sufficiently small β\beta, so (𝐧^,𝐱^)(\hat{\bf n},\hat{\bf x}) is feasible, as claimed. ∎

C.3.2 Proofs from Section 4.3

See 4.3

We first recall the definition of submodular and supermodular set functions.

Definition C.2 (Submodularity/supermodularity).

A set function φ:2𝒯→ℝ\varphi:2^{\mathcal{T}}\to\mathbb{R} is submodular if for all sets SS and S′S^{\prime}

φ⁡(S)+φ⁡(S′)≥φ⁡(S∩S′)+φ⁡(S∪S′).\varphi(S)+\varphi(S^{\prime})\geq\varphi(S\cap S^{\prime})+\varphi(S\cup S^{\prime}). (34)

It is strictly submodular if (34) holds strictly whenever SS and S′S^{\prime} are incomparable (meaning that S⊈S′S\nsubseteq S^{\prime} and S′⊈SS^{\prime}\nsubseteq S). The function φ\varphi is supermodular if −φ-\varphi is submodular, and strictly supermodular if −φ-\varphi is strictly submodular.

Proof.

The program LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has |𝒯|+|ℳ||\mathcal{T}|+|\mathcal{M}| variables, the |𝒯||\mathcal{T}| balance constraints (P-Balance), nonnegativity constraints, and one availability constraint (P-Availability) for every j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T} and nonempty S⊆ℳjS\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}; only the last family is exponentially large. We show how to construct an exact polynomial-time separation oracle for it. Given a point (𝐧^,𝐱^)(\hat{\bf n},\hat{\bf x}), we first check the balance and nonnegativity constraints explicitly. If they hold, then for each j∈𝒯j\in\mathcal{T} we consider the set function

Ψj​(S)=1γS​(λj​γS​∑i∈Sn^i−∑i∈Sx^i​j)=λj​∑i∈Sn^i−1γS​∑i∈Sx^i​j,S⊆ℳj,\Psi_{j}(S)=\frac{1}{\gamma_{S}}\Big(\lambda_{j}\gamma_{S}\sum_{i\in S}\hat{n}_{i}-\sum_{i\in S}\hat{x}_{ij}\Big)=\lambda_{j}\sum_{i\in S}\hat{n}_{i}-\frac{1}{\gamma_{S}}\sum_{i\in S}\hat{x}_{ij},\qquad S\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j},

with Ψj​(∅)=0\Psi_{j}(\emptyset)=0, which is submodular by Lemma 4.3 (the submodularity argument there uses only 𝐱^≥0\hat{\bf x}\geq 0). Since γS>0\gamma_{S}>0, the availability constraint of (S,j)(S,j) holds if and only if Ψj​(S)≥0\Psi_{j}(S)\geq 0, so all availability constraints of jj hold if and only if minS⊆ℳj⁡Ψj​(S)≥0\min_{S\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{j}}\Psi_{j}(S)\geq 0. A submodular function can be minimized in strongly polynomial time (Schrijver 2000), and each evaluation of Ψj\Psi_{j} takes polynomial time. If the minimum is negative, the minimizing set SS identifies a violated constraint, whose defining inequality is a separating hyperplane; otherwise (𝐧^,𝐱^)(\hat{\bf n},\hat{\bf x}) is feasible. By the equivalence of separation and optimization (Grötschel et al. 1988, Theorem 6.4.9), LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) can therefore be solved in polynomial time. ∎

Exact computation: The formula above shows that 𝐅\mathbf{F} is piecewise affine. Two distinct rational numbers with denominators at most 2K2^{K} differ by at least 2−2​K2^{-2K}. This recovers 𝐯ℳ\mathbf{v}^{\mathcal{M}} exactly, in time polynomial in the input size. ∎

C.5.3 Proofs from Section 6.3

See 6.3

Proof.

By the proof of Proposition 4.4 in Section C.3.2, the ellipsoid method, together with an exact polynomial-time separation oracle, solves LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) in polynomial time. Although DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) has a variable zS​jz_{Sj} for each availability constraint, the ellipsoid method applied to LPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{LP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) generates only polynomially many constraints, and a basic optimal solution of DLPPOL​(ℳ)\textup{DLP}^{\textup{POL}}(\mathcal{M}) that is supported on these constraints—hence with polynomially many nonzero weights zS​jz_{Sj}—can be computed in polynomial time (Grötschel et al. 1988, Theorem 6.5.14; see also Lemma 6.5.15 and Theorem 6.5.17). We omit further details for brevity, as this is a standard result. ∎
